scenarios.title: The wildcard that was not
scenarios.situation: A developer's deploy fails: the PKI role 'web' has allowed_domains=example.com and allow_subdomains=true, but issuance for db.internal.example.com is rejected. The developer asks for allow_any_name=true 'to unblock the deploy'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right call?
evidence: common_name=db.internal.example.com. Note: 'internal.example.com' is a SUBDOMAIN of example.com, and 'db' is a subdomain of that — nested subdomains.
choices: Nested subdomains are the issue: allow_subdomains=true permits exactly ONE level (app.example.com), not db.internal.example.com — the correct fix is adding internal.example.com to allowed_domains (with allow_subdomains) or using allow_glob_domains; allow_any_name=true would turn the role into an unrestricted CA
Enable allow_any_name=true; the deploy is blocked and the risk is theoretical
The role is broken; delete it and issue from the root mount directly
Issue with common_name=example.com and use SANs to cover the rest
scenarios.why: Vault's subdomain matching is single-level by default: allow_subdomains covers *.example.com but not *.*.example.com. That is a deliberate safety property, not a bug. allow_any_name=true would let any holder of this role mint certificates for any name in existence — including your bank's domain — which is precisely the forgery capability a CA must never hand out casually. Issuing from the root mount bypasses all policy for convenience, and shoehorning names into SANs on the wrong CN does not change the authorization check. Fix the domain list to reflect the real DNS hierarchy.
scenarios.hint: How many subdomain levels does allow_subdomains=true cover?

scenarios.title: The 90-day cert habit
scenarios.situation: The team issues internal service certificates with 825-day TTLs 'because public CAs used to allow it and renewals are annoying.' Their automation is a quarterly manual ticket. Last quarter the ticket was missed and three services went down on expiry.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct PKI posture?
evidence: Leaf TTL 825 days, manual quarterly renewal ticket, no consul-template, no expiry monitoring. Two outages in a year from expired certs.
Vault can issue any TTL; the team controls the role max_ttl and the automation.
choices: Shorten leaf TTLs drastically (24–72h) AND automate issuance/renewal with consul-template: short TTLs only work with automation, and automation only pays off with short TTLs — the pair eliminates both the expiry outages and the manual ticket
Keep 825-day TTLs but add expiry monitoring and a better ticketing process
Move to 398-day TTLs to match current public CA limits
Issue 10-year certs so renewal is never needed
scenarios.why: Long TTLs plus manual renewal is the worst combination: maximum blast radius per compromised cert AND guaranteed human-error outages. Monitoring a manual process just pages you about the same failure. Copying public-CA limits is cargo-culting — internal PKI exists precisely so you can do better than the public web's constraints. Ten-year certs make revocation your only control and guarantee the CA outlives everyone's memory of it. The correct posture inverts the model: TTLs so short that expiry is routine (hours/days), with automation making renewal invisible. Then a missed renewal is impossible by construction.
scenarios.hint: Why do short TTLs REQUIRE automation — and why is the pair better?

scenarios.title: The revoked cert that kept working
scenarios.situation: A contractor's laptop was stolen. The team promptly revoked the client's VPN certificate in Vault PKI and confirmed the serial on the CRL. A week later, logs show the stolen laptop authenticated to an internal service successfully — with the revoked certificate.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong?
evidence: Serial revoked, CRL rebuilt, CRL DP published at the configured URL. Revocation timestamp correct.
Internal service validates client certs against the CA bundle but never fetches the CRL or configures OCSP — 'we check the signature, that is enough.'
choices: Revocation without checking is theater: the service validates the signature chain but never consults the CRL/OCSP, so the revoked cert verifies fine. Fix: configure the service to check revocation (CRL fetch or OCSP), or move to short-lived certs that expire before revocation matters
The CRL did not propagate; wait longer and it will take effect
Vault revocation is broken; reissue the entire CA
The laptop must have a second, unrevoked certificate
scenarios.why: A signature check answers 'was this issued by our CA?' — it cannot answer 'has this been revoked since?' That second question requires consulting the CRL or OCSP responder, which this service never does. CRL propagation delay is a red herring (a week is not propagation), rebuilding the CA is scorched earth for a client-side checking gap, and inventing a second certificate is speculation. The lesson generalizes: every revocation story has two halves — publishing the revocation AND clients checking it. Audit both halves. For services that cannot check revocation reliably, short TTLs (hours) bound the exposure window by construction.
scenarios.hint: What two halves make up a working revocation story?

scenarios.title: The intermediate key scare
scenarios.situation: A backup of the Vault storage was found on an unencrypted USB drive. The backup contains the PKI intermediate's private key. The offline root is safe in the HSM. The CISO asks: do we need to rotate every certificate in the company?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
evidence: Intermediate private key for pki_int (signs all service certs) on unencrypted media, custody unknown for 3 weeks. Root CA (offline, HSM) not exposed.
~4,000 active leaf certs, TTLs 24h–7d, automated renewal via consul-template. CRL/OCSP infrastructure exists and clients check.
choices: Yes for the intermediate, no panic for the leaves: generate a new intermediate (new key), cross-sign or re-chain clients to trust it, revoke the old intermediate, and let the short-TTL leaves rotate naturally within days — the root stays, the chain of trust is rebuilt below it. This is exactly the scenario the offline-root/online-intermediate topology exists for
No action needed; the root is safe so the chain is safe
Rotate the root CA immediately and reissue all 4,000 certs by hand
Just revoke the intermediate and continue; clients will figure out the new chain
scenarios.why: An exposed intermediate key means an attacker can mint valid certificates for your trust domain — 'the root is safe' does not help because clients trust the chain through the intermediate. Doing nothing bets the company on the USB drive being unread. Rotating the root is unnecessary upheaval: the root's whole purpose is staying offline while intermediates take the operational risk. Revoking without a replacement chain breaks every service at once. The designed response: new intermediate, clients trust the new chain (cross-signing smooths the transition), revoke the old, and short leaf TTLs mean the leaf population turns over within days automatically. Then find out how a storage backup reached a USB drive.
scenarios.hint: Why does the offline-root/online-intermediate topology exist?

scenarios.title: The mystery certificate
scenarios.situation: A developer finds a valid certificate for api.example.com in a public transparency log that nobody on the team issued. The Vault PKI mount is the only internal CA. The certificate validates against your root.
scenarios.prompt: What does this indicate and what do you do?
evidence: Certificate in public CT log, signed by your intermediate, CN=api.example.com, issued 2 days ago. Vault audit shows pki_int/issue/web called by a token belonging to a decommissioned CI service account.
The CI account was decommissioned 6 months ago but its Vault token was periodic with no expiry. Role 'web' has allow_subdomains=true.
choices: An unauthorized issuance via a zombie credential: the decommissioned CI account's never-expiring token was used (or stolen and used) to mint a cert. Revoke the token and its leases, revoke the certificate, audit ALL issuances by that token, fix the role to least privilege, and kill periodic tokens for decommissioned workloads — then find how the token leaked
The CT log is wrong; ignore it since the team did not issue the cert
Revoke the certificate; the problem is solved
Rotate the intermediate CA; the token issue is secondary
scenarios.why: The certificate is real — it validates against your root, so your CA issued it, and the audit log names the caller. Dismissing the CT log is denial; revoking only the cert leaves the zombie token minting replacements; rotating the CA treats the symptom (untrusted certs) while the disease (immortal token) persists. The full response: kill the credential, revoke what it minted, audit its entire history (what else did it issue in 6 months?), remove the conditions (periodic tokens for dead workloads, over-broad roles), and investigate the leak. CT logs are a detective control — this is them working. Monitor issuance logs the same way going forward.
scenarios.hint: What does a certificate in a CT log that you did not issue prove?

scenarios.title: The storage that never shrinks
scenarios.situation: Vault storage has grown 40% in a year. Investigation shows the pki_int mount's storage holds every certificate ever issued — 2 million entries — including certs expired years ago. Issuance latency is climbing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
evidence: pki_int: 2M stored certs, ~90% expired. tidy never configured. Issuance p99 up 3x.
Compliance requires retaining revocation evidence for revoked-but-unexpired certs; expired certs have no retention requirement.
choices: Configure and schedule tidy: vault write pki_int/config/urls + tidy with tidy_cert_store and safety_buffer — tidy removes expired certs and expired CRL entries while preserving revocation data for unexpired certs; run it on a schedule and watch storage and latency recover
Delete the oldest certs directly from storage with API calls
Add more storage; growth is normal
Disable certificate storage (no_store=true) going forward
scenarios.why: PKI mounts accumulate every issued certificate by default — without tidy, storage grows forever and issuance slows as the store bloats. Hand-deleting from storage bypasses the safety logic (you could delete revocation evidence for unexpired certs, breaking compliance). Adding storage treats growth as acceptable when it is operational waste. no_store helps future issuance but does nothing for the 2M rows already there — and it destroys your issuance inventory. Tidy is the designed mechanism: it respects the safety buffer, keeps revocation records for unexpired certs, and purges what compliance allows. Schedule it; do not run it once and forget.
scenarios.hint: What does PKI tidy remove — and what does it deliberately keep?

scenarios.title: The intermediate expires Friday
scenarios.situation: The pki_int intermediate CA expires in 5 days. It was created 3 years ago with a 3-year TTL and nobody calendarized rotation. 4,000 services get leaf certs from it via consul-template with 24h TTLs.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct emergency rotation?
evidence: Root (10y, safe) -> pki_int (expires in 5d) -> 4,000 leaves (24h TTL, auto-renewed). Clients trust root + intermediate bundle.
If pki_int expires, every leaf chain breaks simultaneously regardless of leaf TTL — 4,000 services down.
choices: Generate the new intermediate NOW under the same root, publish the new chain bundle to clients (cross-sign period where both intermediates are trusted), point issuance at the new intermediate, and let 24h leaf TTLs roll the fleet onto the new chain within a day — then revoke the old intermediate after expiry. Calendarize the next rotation immediately
Extend the intermediate's TTL with a config change to buy time
Reissue all 4,000 leaf certs manually before Friday
Let it expire and reissue; the outage will force the automation to be fixed
scenarios.why: CA TTLs cannot be extended after issuance — the expiry is baked into the certificate; 'buying time' is impossible. Manual reissuance of 4,000 certs in 5 days is a human-error factory. Letting it expire to 'teach a lesson' is sabotage. The correct move uses the architecture: the root is fine, so mint a fresh intermediate under it; distribute the new chain while the old still validates (overlap, not flag day); issuance flips to the new intermediate; short leaf TTLs migrate the fleet automatically within 24 hours. The real fix is the calendar entry and the rehearsal — rotation must be a practiced routine, not a fire drill.
scenarios.hint: Can a CA certificate's TTL be extended after issuance?

scenarios.title: The decrypt-everything service
scenarios.situation: The reporting service needs to encrypt PII before writing to the data warehouse. Its Vault policy grants transit/encrypt/orders AND transit/decrypt/orders 'because the SDK example used both.' The service was compromised last week; attackers exfiltrated the warehouse's ciphertext column.
scenarios.prompt: What is the policy failure and the correct scoping?
evidence: paths transit/encrypt/orders and transit/decrypt/orders: [update]. Service writes ciphertexts; never legitimately reads plaintext.
With decrypt capability, the compromised service could have decrypted the entire warehouse column — ciphertext exfiltration becomes plaintext exfiltration.
choices: Encrypt and decrypt are separate privileges: the reporting service should hold ONLY transit/encrypt/orders. Decrypt belongs to the narrow set of readers with business need. The exfiltrated ciphertext is opaque without decrypt — scoping is what makes stolen ciphertext useless
The policy is fine; the compromise is a network security problem
Remove transit access entirely and encrypt in the application
Rotate the transit key; that fixes the exposure
scenarios.why: This is the transit equivalent of giving every service the database password: the SDK example's convenience became a standing decryption capability. With decrypt, ciphertext theft equals plaintext theft — the entire point of field-level encryption (stolen dumps stay opaque) collapses. Blaming the network misses that Vault policies are the last line of defense precisely for compromised services. Removing transit forces every app to manage keys (worse). Rotating the key does not revoke the attacker's decrypt capability on new data. Least privilege per direction: writers encrypt, readers decrypt, almost nobody does both.
scenarios.hint: Why are transit encrypt and decrypt separate capabilities?

scenarios.title: The rotation that was not
scenarios.situation: Compliance asks for proof of annual encryption-key rotation. The team ran 'vault write -f transit/keys/orders/rotate' last month and declared compliance. But the warehouse's PII column — 800M rows encrypted over 3 years — was never re-encrypted.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the compliance claim?
evidence: orders: 4 versions. min_decryption_version=1. 800M rows: ~95% still vault:v1: ciphertext.
'Key rotated annually' — true for NEW encryptions only.
choices: Rotation without rewrap is incomplete: old ciphertexts still use v1, so the 'retired' key version must remain decryptable forever — the rotation protected only new data. True rotation = rotate + rewrap existing ciphertexts (transit/rewrap) + raise min_decryption_version only after rewrap completes
The claim is valid; rotation applies to the key, not the data
Delete key version 1 to force compliance
Re-encrypting 800M rows is infeasible; accept the risk
scenarios.why: Key rotation has two halves: minting the new version (done) and migrating existing ciphertexts to it (not done). With 95% of data still on v1, the old key material remains live and must stay decryptable — the rotation is cosmetic for the data that matters. Deleting v1 now would crypto-shred 760M rows (the data becomes permanently unreadable). 'Infeasible' is a planning failure: rewrap is a batch job, run it incrementally. The compliance-correct sequence: rotate → rewrap in batches with verification → confirm zero v1 ciphertexts remain → raise min_decryption_version → then claim rotation.
scenarios.hint: What are the two halves of a complete key rotation?

scenarios.title: The searchable encryption trap
scenarios.situation: The team wants to query encrypted emails with WHERE clauses, so they enable convergent encryption on the email field 'to keep queries working.' Emails are attacker-guessable (firstname.lastname@example.com patterns).
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk?
evidence: transit key with derived=true, convergent_encryption=true, per-field context=tenant-id.
2M emails, highly structured and guessable. Attackers get the ciphertext column via a SQL injection in the reporting tool (read-only).
choices: Convergent encryption is deterministic: identical plaintexts produce identical ciphertexts. With guessable emails, attackers encrypt guesses and compare — an offline dictionary attack against the column. Fix: use convergent ONLY where equality queries are required AND the plaintext has high entropy, or redesign to tokenize emails (random tokens + encrypted mapping) instead
There is no risk; convergent encryption is still AES
The risk is the SQL injection, not the encryption mode
Add a longer context string to fix it
scenarios.why: Deterministic encryption trades semantic security for queryability: the ciphertext leaks equality, and for low-entropy plaintexts equality is enough to brute-force. AES strength is irrelevant — the attack never breaks AES, it just re-encrypts guesses (the attacker has the algorithm; only the key is secret, and comparison needs no key). The SQL injection is a separate bug, but defense in depth means the ciphertext should resist even when stolen. Longer contexts do not add entropy against guessing the PLAINTEXT. The right call: convergent only for high-entropy fields needing equality, tokenization (random, non-deterministic) for guessable PII.
scenarios.hint: What does deterministic ciphertext leak, and against what data is that fatal?

scenarios.title: The million-row timeout
scenarios.situation: A backfill job tokenizes 5M PII records via transit, one API call per record. It has been running 14 hours, the Vault leader is saturated, and the job is 30% done. The deadline is tomorrow.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
evidence: Sequential single encrypt calls, ~40ms each with network. 5M * 40ms = ~55 hours. Leader CPU 95% from request volume.
Transit supports batch_input: up to N operations per HTTP call.
choices: Batch the operations: transit's batch_input packs hundreds of encryptions per request, collapsing 5M round trips into ~10k calls — the job finishes in under an hour and the leader breathes. Also consider parallelism across standby nodes for reads and scheduling backfills off-peak
Add more Vault nodes to handle the load
Increase the HTTP timeout so the job can run 55 hours
Encrypt in the application instead to bypass Vault
scenarios.why: The bottleneck is round trips, not crypto: 40ms × 5M is pure latency arithmetic. More nodes do not reduce per-request latency for writes (they all funnel to the leader). Longer timeouts just let the slow job be slow. Bypassing Vault abandons key management for speed — the classic security-for-performance trade that creates the next incident. Batching is the designed solution: same security properties, ~500x fewer round trips. Generalize the lesson: any bulk Vault workflow (tokenization, rewrap, migration) must use batch APIs, or the job becomes a self-inflicted DoS on the cluster.
scenarios.hint: What dominates the runtime of 5M single API calls — crypto or round trips?

scenarios.title: The export request
scenarios.situation: A vendor's migration tool 'requires' the transit private key exported in plaintext to migrate encrypted data to their platform. They ask you to enable key export on the production HSM-backed key.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
evidence: HSM-backed, export disabled at creation. Compliance regime: keys must not leave the HSM.
'Our tool needs the raw key; every customer does this.' No alternative offered.
choices: Refuse export; offer the secure migration path: re-encrypt via Vault (decrypt with old key, encrypt with a migration key the vendor CAN'T export either — or run the migration inside your boundary with the vendor's tool operating on plaintext it receives transiently). Enabling export on an HSM key violates the compliance regime and creates an exfiltration capability that persists after the vendor leaves
Enable export temporarily, then disable it after the migration
Export the key; the vendor is a trusted partner
Copy the key to a software key first, then export that
scenarios.why: 'Temporary' export cannot be un-seen: once key material leaves the HSM in plaintext, every copy (vendor systems, backups, logs) is outside your control forever, and toggling the flag back changes nothing. Trusting the vendor confuses business trust with key custody — the compliance regime exists precisely to survive trusted parties. Copying to a software key first is export with extra steps and the same violation. The professional answer: migrations happen through re-encryption workflows where the key never moves — decrypt/re-encrypt inside your boundary, or issue the vendor scoped decrypt-only access during the window. If the vendor truly cannot work without raw keys, that is a vendor-selection signal.
scenarios.hint: Why is 'temporary' key export a permanent decision?

scenarios.title: The plaintext next to the ciphertext
scenarios.situation: Code review finds: app calls transit/datakey, encrypts a file with the plaintext DEK, then stores the PLAINTEXT DEK in the database 'for convenience' next to the ciphertext DEK. 'It is fine, the database is encrypted at rest.'
scenarios.prompt: What is broken?
evidence: datakey/plaintext/orders → plaintext DEK in DB column dek_plaintext, ciphertext DEK in dek_wrapped. File encrypted with DEK.
'Database encrypted at rest' — one KMS key for the whole DB, held by the cloud provider.
choices: The envelope is open: storing the plaintext DEK next to the data destroys the entire envelope-encryption model — anyone reading the DB row gets key and ciphertext together. The plaintext DEK must exist only in memory during the operation; only the WRAPPED (transit-encrypted) DEK is stored. Database-at-rest encryption protects against stolen disks, not against DB readers
Nothing; database encryption at rest covers it
The DEK should be longer
Use transit/encrypt directly instead of datakey
scenarios.why: Envelope encryption's security rests on one rule: the plaintext data-key never persists. Storing it in the DB column next to the wrapped copy means every DB reader — backups, replicas, analysts, SQL-injection attackers — gets decryption for free. Database-at-rest encryption is a different layer (stolen-disk protection) and does not constrain DB readers at all. Key length is irrelevant when the key is published. Direct transit/encrypt would avoid the pattern but the app chose envelope for large files — the fix is using it correctly: plaintext DEK in memory only, wrapped DEK stored, and ideally the app never sees the plaintext DEK at all (use the transit-provided rewrap/decrypt flows).
scenarios.hint: What is the one rule of envelope encryption?

scenarios.title: The unsigned webhook
scenarios.situation: A payment webhook receiver accepts callbacks and acts on them. Twice, forged callbacks triggered refunds. The team proposes signing webhooks with a transit ed25519 key and verifying signatures on receipt.
scenarios.prompt: Is this the right use of transit, and what completes the design?
evidence: transit key type ed25519; signer service signs payload, receiver verifies via transit/verify.
No replay protection designed; signatures cover the payload only.
choices: Yes, transit signing is the right primitive — but signatures alone are insufficient: add timestamps/nonces and reject old or replayed payloads, bind the signature to the full request (payload + timestamp), and scope the verify capability separately from sign. Otherwise attackers replay a captured valid callback
No — use HMAC with a shared secret instead; transit is overkill
Yes, signatures alone solve it; deploy as planned
No — webhooks cannot be secured, use polling instead
scenarios.why: Transit ed25519 signing is exactly right: the signing key never leaves Vault, verification is a policy-scoped API call, and rotation is centralized. But a valid signature on a replayed payload still verifies — the attacker does not forge, they replay. HMAC with a shared secret recreates key-distribution problems transit was chosen to avoid. 'Signatures alone' ships the replay hole. Polling instead of webhooks is architecture surrender. Complete design: sign(payload || timestamp || nonce), receiver rejects timestamps older than 5 minutes and caches seen nonces, sign and verify capabilities on separate policies, and alert on verification failures (they are attack telemetry).
scenarios.hint: What attack survives a valid signature, and what defeats it?

scenarios.title: The two-node cluster
scenarios.situation: A startup runs Vault with 2 Raft nodes 'for HA.' During a routine kernel upgrade, one node reboots. The cluster stops serving writes for 4 minutes until the node returns.
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural error?
evidence: Single node reboot → no leader → writes rejected for 4 min. Reads on standbys also affected (forwarding to no leader).
choices: Even-numbered Raft clusters gain no fault tolerance: 2 nodes need 2 for quorum (majority of 2 is 2), so ANY single failure halts writes — it is worse than 1 node (same availability, double the cost and complexity). Run 3 nodes across failure domains; 3 tolerates 1 failure, which is the actual HA bar
The reboot was too slow; tune the kernel upgrade process
Vault should have failed over to the second node automatically
Add a third node as a non-voter to break ties
scenarios.why: Raft quorum is majority: for 2 nodes that is 2, meaning zero failures tolerated — the 'HA' cluster has strictly worse availability characteristics than advertised and all the operational cost of clustering. There is no automatic failover that fixes math: the surviving node cannot elect itself leader without quorum. A non-voting node does not count toward quorum and changes nothing. Faster reboots shrink the window but the design still halts on any single failure. The rule is simple and absolute: Raft clusters are 3 or 5 voters, odd, spread across failure domains. Two nodes is never the answer.
scenarios.hint: What is the quorum of a 2-node Raft cluster, and what does that imply?

scenarios.title: The split brain that was not
scenarios.situation: A network partition isolates vault-3 from vault-1 and vault-2 for 90 seconds. vault-3's logs show 'failed to contact quorum, stepping down.' The team panics about split-brain writes.
scenarios.prompt: Did split-brain occur, and why not?
evidence: vault-3: no leader contact for 90s, stepped down to follower, rejected writes. vault-1/2: maintained quorum, elected/kept leader, served writes.
Partition heals; vault-3 rejoins as follower, replicates the log, no conflicts.
choices: No split-brain: Raft's quorum rule prevented it — the isolated single node could not reach majority, so it stepped down and refused writes, while the 2-node majority kept exactly one leader. This is the design working: partitions cause unavailability on the minority side, never divergent writes
Yes, split-brain occurred; reconcile the divergent logs manually
The 90-second window was too short for split-brain; longer partitions would diverge
Autopilot prevented it; without autopilot it would have split
scenarios.why: Split-brain requires two sides both believing they are authoritative — Raft makes that impossible by requiring majority for leadership and for every write. The isolated node did the only safe thing: without quorum contact it abdicated and went read-rejecting. Duration is irrelevant: a 90-minute partition behaves identically, the minority just stays unavailable longer. Autopilot cleans up dead voters but plays no role in partition safety — the quorum math does. The operational takeaway: partitions in Raft cost availability on the minority side, never consistency. Design clients to retry against the majority side.
scenarios.hint: Why can a Raft minority never elect a leader?

scenarios.title: The mystery elections
scenarios.situation: The cluster elects a new leader 3–4 times per day at random times. No deploys, no network events correlate. Metrics show vault-1's disk fsync latency spiking to 800ms during the events; the other nodes are at 2ms. vault-1 is on a shared cloud volume.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and fix?
evidence: Leader elections correlate exactly with fsync spikes on vault-1 (the leader each time). Raft heartbeat timeouts fire because the leader cannot fsync heartbeats in time.
vault-1 on shared/network volume; vault-2/3 on local SSD.
choices: Slow disk on the leader: Raft heartbeats require timely fsync; 800ms fsync latency makes followers declare the leader dead and elect anew. Fix the storage — move vault-1 to local SSD like its peers — and consider loosening heartbeat timeouts only as a secondary measure. Never 'fix' elections by raising timeouts to mask bad disks
Increase election timeouts so the slow disk stops triggering elections
The network is flaky; investigate the switches
Add more nodes so elections matter less
scenarios.why: Raft is a timing-sensitive protocol over durable storage: the leader must persist log entries and heartbeats within timeout windows. An 800ms fsync on a shared volume blows those windows, so followers correctly conclude the leader is dead — the elections are the system working as designed around broken infrastructure. Raising timeouts masks the symptom while writes get slower for everyone (every write waits on that disk). The network is innocent (metrics indict the disk). More nodes do not fix a slow leader; they just give you more witnesses. Raft nodes need provisioned, low-latency, dedicated disks — this is a hard infrastructure requirement, not a tuning preference.
scenarios.hint: Why does slow disk cause leader elections?

scenarios.title: The dead voter
scenarios.situation: vault-3's host died permanently 6 months ago. The cluster runs fine on vault-1/2. Today vault-1 needs a kernel reboot. The team realizes: with vault-3 dead and vault-1 rebooting, only vault-2 remains — no quorum.
scenarios.prompt: What happened operationally, and what prevents recurrence?
evidence: list-peers: vault-1, vault-2 active; vault-3 'alive=false' for 6 months. Autopilot disabled ('we will clean up manually').
3 voters, 1 dead → quorum needs 2 of 3. Rebooting vault-1 leaves 1 of 3 — cluster halts.
choices: Voter-set rot: the dead node was never removed, so the cluster has been running without real fault tolerance for 6 months — any second failure halts it. Fix now: remove vault-3 as a peer (or replace the host and rejoin), then enable autopilot with dead-server cleanup so this can never silently recur
Reboot vault-1 anyway; 1 of 3 nodes can elect itself in an emergency
Add vault-4 and vault-5 to restore redundancy
Restore vault-3 from snapshot to get quorum back
scenarios.why: The cluster's fault tolerance quietly decayed to zero months ago: with one dead voter, quorum math (2 of 3) means the NEXT single failure is fatal — and nobody noticed because reads/writes kept working. A lone node cannot elect itself (majority of 3 is 2, always). Adding nodes to a degraded cluster without removing the dead voter just grows the voter set around the corpse. Restoring from snapshot resurrects stale state unnecessarily. The fix is hygiene: remove/replace dead voters promptly, and enable autopilot so dead-server removal is automatic, not a calendar item humans forget. Monitor voter health as a tier-1 check.
scenarios.hint: What is voter-set rot, and why is it silent?

scenarios.title: The join that hangs
scenarios.situation: A new node vault-4 runs 'vault operator raft join https://vault-1:8201' and hangs indefinitely. Logs show TLS handshake errors: 'certificate is not valid for vault-4.internal'. The existing 3 nodes are healthy.
scenarios.prompt: What is misconfigured?
evidence: Node certs issued with SANs for vault-1..3 only. vault-4 reuses vault-1's certificate files (copied during provisioning).
choices: Certificate identity mismatch: vault-4 presents vault-1's certificate, whose SANs do not include vault-4.internal — mutual TLS verification fails and the join hangs. Each node needs its own certificate with its own SANs (ideally auto-issued from the PKI engine with short TTLs)
The join address is wrong; use HTTP instead
Raft join requires unsealing vault-4 first with the leader's keys
The cluster is full at 3 nodes; Raft cannot add a fourth
scenarios.why: Raft cluster traffic is mutual TLS: each node authenticates the peer's certificate against expected identities. A copied cert means vault-4 claims to be vault-1 while advertising node_id vault-4 — verification fails, correctly. Falling back to HTTP 'fixes' the hang by deleting the security. Unseal order is unrelated to TLS handshake failures. Raft absolutely supports adding voters (3→5 is standard). The systemic fix: stop copying certificate files in provisioning; issue per-node certs with correct SANs, ideally from Vault's own PKI engine with automation, so new nodes are born with valid identity.
scenarios.hint: Why does copying one node's TLS cert to another break the join?

scenarios.title: The restore onto live
scenarios.situation: After a bad policy change locked out the admins, an operator decides to 'restore yesterday's snapshot' — and runs 'vault operator raft snapshot restore' against the LIVE cluster's active node.
scenarios.prompt: What happens, and what should they have done?
evidence: Snapshot restore issued to the active node of a running 3-node cluster.
Restore is a rebuild operation: stop Vault, restore on fresh nodes, unseal. Not supported against live members.
choices: The restore is rejected/unsupported against a live active node — and attempting it risks the running cluster. Correct path: the lockout is a POLICY problem, not a data problem — use the root token or recovery keys to fix the policy (generate a new root via unseal keys if needed). Snapshots are for data loss/disaster, not for access lockouts; restore means rebuilding the cluster from the snapshot on fresh nodes
The restore succeeds and rolls back the policy change
The restore merges the snapshot with live data
Restart all nodes first, then restore onto the live cluster
scenarios.why: Two confusions compound here. First, restores do not run against live clusters — Raft restore replaces the node's entire dataset, which is incoherent on a running member; it is a disaster-recovery rebuild primitive. Second, the actual problem (admin lockout via policy) never needed a restore: unseal/recovery keys can generate a new root token, and root can repair any policy. Reaching for the snapshot was using the heaviest tool for a light problem — and a day-old snapshot would also have rolled back every secret rotation since. Match the tool to the problem: lockout → recovery keys; data loss → snapshot rebuild on fresh nodes.
scenarios.hint: When is a snapshot restore the right tool — and when is it not?

scenarios.title: The standby that serves stale reads
scenarios.situation: The team enabled performance standbys and pointed a reporting job at a standby for 'faster reads.' The job intermittently shows secrets rotated minutes ago as still old. They blame replication lag and want to disable perf standbys.
scenarios.prompt: What is actually happening, and what is the right fix?
evidence: Standby serves reads from local state; writes forward to active. Replication of the Raft log to standbys is fast but not instantaneous.
Reads a just-rotated secret within seconds of rotation; sometimes gets the pre-rotation value. No consistency requirement was set.
choices: Eventual consistency on standbys: a standby's local state can lag the active by milliseconds-to-seconds — reads immediately after a write may be stale. This is the documented trade-off, not a bug. Fix: route consistency-sensitive reads (read-after-write) to the active node; keep analytics and tolerant reads on standbys. Disabling perf standbys throws away the scaling benefit for a workload-routing mistake
Replication is broken; rebuild the standby
Perf standbys are eventually removed; migrate off
Increase the rotation interval so staleness windows do not matter
scenarios.why: Performance standbys trade read freshness for scale — that is their entire purpose. Expecting linearizable reads from a standby is expecting the feature to not be the feature. Rebuilding a healthy standby wastes a day; the 'staleness' is working as designed. Changing rotation intervals to accommodate a reader inverts the dependency (writers serve readers' convenience). The correct architecture: classify reads by consistency need. Read-after-write flows (just rotated, now read) go to the active; bulk analytics and cache-friendly reads go to standbys. One routing rule, documented per workload, replaces the incident.
scenarios.hint: What consistency do performance standbys provide, and how should reads be routed?

scenarios.title: The secret in the wrong tenant
scenarios.situation: A deploy script writes canary values to secret/canary without a namespace flag. The platform team runs it from a root-namespace admin token 'because it needs to cover all tenants.' Yesterday a tenant reported seeing another tenant's canary value.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong?
evidence: vault kv put secret/canary/app value=... — no -namespace flag, root token.
team-a and team-b each have their own secret/ mount; the script wrote to ROOT's secret/ mount. Tenant dashboards were pointed at root's mount 'temporarily.'
choices: The script wrote to the root namespace's mount (no -namespace flag defaults to the token's namespace — root), and tenant tooling was pointed at that shared mount: a cross-tenant data leak through namespace confusion. Fix: namespace-scoped tokens per tenant, -namespace on every command, tenant dashboards pointed at their own mounts, and never use root tokens in automation
KV v2 is leaking across namespaces; file a bug
The tenants' mounts are misconfigured; remount them
Canary values are not sensitive; ignore the report
scenarios.why: Namespaces only isolate when you actually use them: a missing -namespace flag silently targets the token's own namespace, and a root token's namespace is root — shared by definition. Nothing leaked 'across' namespaces; the data was written to a shared location and tenants were pointed at it. That is three failures: automation with root tokens, missing namespace flags, and tenant tooling aimed at root. The report is a real incident regardless of canary sensitivity — the same path carries real secrets. Remediation is mechanical (scoped tokens, explicit flags, correct dashboard targets) plus a sweep for other root-token automation.
scenarios.hint: What namespace does a command target when no -namespace flag is given?

scenarios.title: The delegated admin who escaped
scenarios.situation: A namespace admin for team-a holds a policy granting 'team-a/*' with sudo in the ROOT namespace 'so they can manage their namespace.' Audit shows them reading secret/ mounts in team-b's namespace yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the policy error?
evidence: Token used against team-b's mounts successfully. team-a/* in root covers the NAMESPACE DEFINITION path, not the namespace's contents — but sudo + broad API access enabled sys/namespace-adjacent escapes.
choices: The delegation model is wrong: namespace contents are managed from WITHIN the namespace, not via root paths. team-a/* in root governs the namespace object itself, not team-a's secrets — and sudo in root is a skeleton key. Correct: create an admin policy INSIDE the team-a namespace (path "*" within that namespace context) and grant it to the admin's entity there; root retains nothing for them
The admin is malicious; revoke and investigate (only)
Namespaces are broken; flatten to a single namespace
Add a deny stanza for team-b/* to the same policy
scenarios.why: This is a namespace-model misunderstanding with a sudo-shaped hole: in Vault, you administer a namespace's contents with policies created inside that namespace, not with root-namespace paths that happen to share a name prefix. team-a/* at root is the namespace's management API surface, while sudo anywhere near root is effectively administrative access to everything. A deny carve-out is whack-a-mole against a structurally wrong grant. The person may or may not be malicious — but the system made escape trivially easy, so fix the system: in-namespace admin policies, no root sudo for tenant admins, and audit what the over-broad grant already touched.
scenarios.hint: Where should a namespace admin's policy live — root or the namespace?

scenarios.title: The eleven break-glass accounts
scenarios.situation: The org has 11 namespaces, each with its own userpass mount and break-glass admin 'for isolation.' Password rotation is manual. Three of the passwords are past due, and nobody knows who holds two of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct identity architecture?
evidence: 11 userpass mounts, 11 break-glass passwords, spreadsheet-tracked, 3 overdue.
Emergency access per namespace + normal admin workflows.
choices: Centralize: one identity source (OIDC/LDAP at root or per-namespace auth pointing at the same directory), identity GROUPS spanning namespaces for the platform team, and a SINGLE break-glass procedure (root recovery keys / sealed Shamir shares) instead of 11 passwords. Per-namespace userpass multiplies the credential count without adding real isolation — it adds 11 unmanaged secrets
Automate the 11 password rotations with a script
Consolidate to one namespace to reduce the count
Store the 11 passwords in Vault itself
scenarios.why: Eleven break-glass accounts is eleven standing privileged credentials with manual rotation — the 'isolation' rationale confuses credential count with security. Automation would make the bad pattern run on time, not make it good. Flattening namespaces destroys the tenancy model to fix an identity problem. Storing the passwords in Vault is circular (the break-glass for Vault lives in Vault). The right architecture separates concerns: humans authenticate via the central directory (one deprovisioning point), platform admins get cross-namespace access via identity groups, and true break-glass is the root recovery mechanism (Shamir shares / KMS), not a password. Fewer credentials, each with an owner and a rotation story.
scenarios.hint: Why is one break-glass mechanism better than eleven?

scenarios.title: The noisy neighbor
scenarios.situation: team-c runs a load test that mints 50k tokens; the shared cluster's token store latency spikes and team-a's deploys start failing. Namespaces isolated the DATA but not the shared control plane.
scenarios.prompt: What is the missing control?
evidence: Token creation latency 10x during team-c's test. team-a deploy failures (token creation timeouts). Same cluster, different namespaces.
No rate limits or quotas configured. All namespaces share the token store and request path.
choices: Namespaces are a data-isolation boundary, not a performance-isolation boundary: the fix is rate limiting and quotas — per-namespace rate-limit quotas (requests/sec) and lease-count quotas cap each tenant's control-plane consumption so one tenant's load test cannot starve others
Move team-c to its own cluster immediately
Namespaces are insufficient; abandon them
Increase the cluster size to absorb the load
scenarios.why: This is the noisy-neighbor problem every multi-tenant control plane has: logical isolation (namespaces) without resource isolation (quotas). A dedicated cluster per team 'solves' it at maximum cost and operational sprawl — premature for a load-test incident. Abandoning namespaces over a missing quota is architectural panic. Bigger clusters raise the ceiling but a bigger load test hits it again. Vault's designed answer is quotas: rate-limit quotas bound requests/sec per namespace, lease-count quotas bound total leases. Set them from observed baselines, alert before enforcing, and give tenants a quota-increase process. Isolation must be engineered at every layer, not assumed from one.
scenarios.hint: What do namespaces isolate — and what do they NOT isolate?

scenarios.title: The hundred policies
scenarios.situation: Each of 40 teams needs an identical 'standard-reader' policy in their namespace. The platform team hand-writes 40 copies. Three have drifted (one grants delete). A new team onboarded last week still has no policy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the sustainable pattern?
evidence: 40 policy files, 3 drifted, 1 team missing. Onboarding is a manual ticket.
Policies applied by hand via CLI; no git, no CI.
choices: Policy as code with templating: one standard-reader template, rendered per namespace and applied via CI on every change — drift becomes impossible (CI reapplies), onboarding is a parameter (new namespace = new render), and the delete-granting drift gets caught in code review, not in an incident
Hire someone to manage the 40 policies
Give all teams one shared policy in the root namespace
Reduce the number of teams
scenarios.why: Hand-managed duplicated policy is configuration drift with a countdown timer: the three drifted copies prove humans cannot maintain N identical files, and the missing onboarding proves the process does not scale. More headcount scales the toil linearly. A shared root policy breaks tenant isolation (one policy change affects everyone, no per-tenant variation possible). Fewer teams is not a lever the platform team owns. The sustainable pattern is the standard one: single template, parameterized render, CI-applied, git-reviewed. Then 'add a team' is a one-line change and 'audit all policies' is reading one file.
scenarios.hint: How do you keep 40 identical policies identical?

scenarios.title: The mount maze
scenarios.situation: Across namespaces, teams mounted engines at creative paths: team-a uses secrets/, team-b uses kv/, team-c uses prod-secrets-v2/. Automation that works in one namespace breaks in others. New hires cannot find anything.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
evidence: 47 mounts across 11 namespaces, 9 distinct naming conventions for the same KV use case.
Every runbook needs per-namespace path translation; onboarding takes weeks.
choices: A mount-path convention enforced at provisioning: e.g., every namespace gets secret/ (kv-v2), transit/ (transit), pki_int/ (pki) — same paths everywhere, provisioned by automation, not by team creativity. Then migrate existing mounts (secrets move) on a schedule and document the standard
Let teams keep their paths; write a lookup service
Merge all namespaces so paths are unique
Rename mounts freely; paths do not matter
scenarios.why: Mount paths are API: inconsistent APIs across tenants make every automation, runbook, and onboarding namespace-aware in the worst way. A lookup service adds a dependency to paper over sprawl. Merging namespaces destroys tenancy to fix naming. 'Paths do not matter' is false — policies, audit queries, and human memory all key on paths. The fix is boring and effective: a standard layout, enforced by the provisioning automation that creates namespaces (teams do not hand-create mounts), plus a migration window for the creative legacy. Conventions are infrastructure.
scenarios.hint: Why are mount paths API?

scenarios.title: The invisible tenant
scenarios.situation: Compliance asks: 'Show us all human access to production secrets in Q3.' The platform team produces root-namespace audit logs — but team-a's namespace audit was never enabled, and its logs only exist in the namespace's own device, which nobody collected.
scenarios.prompt: What is the audit architecture gap?
evidence: Audit devices enabled in root only. 11 namespaces, 0 with their own audit devices. Assumption was 'root audit covers everything.'
Requests in a namespace are audited by THAT namespace's devices; root's devices do not see them. Q3 tenant access is unlogged.
choices: Audit devices are per-namespace: each namespace needs its own audit device (or explicit forwarding), shipping to the central SIEM. The 'root covers everything' assumption is false — namespace-scoped requests never touch root's audit path. Remediate: enable and verify audit in every namespace, centralize collection, and add 'audit enabled' to the namespace provisioning checklist
Enable one global audit device; it will catch up retroactively
Namespaces cannot be audited; flatten them
Accept the gap; Q3 is over
scenarios.why: Audit in Vault follows the request's namespace, not the administrator's hopes: a request authenticated in team-a is logged by team-a's audit devices, period. No retroactive capture exists — unlogged Q3 access is unlogged forever, which is itself a compliance finding. Flattening namespaces to fix auditing inverts the priority (tenancy serves the business; audit serves compliance — serve both). Accepting the gap fails the audit. The architecture: audit devices as part of namespace provisioning (automation, not memory), all shipping to central collection, with a monitor that alerts when any namespace lacks a healthy audit device. Add it to the provisioning checklist so namespace #12 is born compliant.
scenarios.hint: Which audit devices see a request made in team-a's namespace?

scenarios.title: The localhost that was not
scenarios.situation: The payments service runs a Connect sidecar, but its app binds to 0.0.0.0:8443 'for debugging.' A compromised container on the same host connects directly to payments:8443, bypassing the sidecar — and the intentions, and the mTLS.
scenarios.prompt: What is the misconfiguration?
evidence: Connect sidecar registered, intentions default-deny with payments allowed only from orders. App binds 0.0.0.0:8443.
Lateral connection to :8443 succeeded with no client cert; intentions never evaluated (traffic never entered the mesh).
choices: The app must bind to localhost only: binding 0.0.0.0 exposes the plaintext port to the host network, letting anyone bypass the sidecar proxy — and with it the mTLS identity and intentions. The mesh's security properties only hold for traffic that actually traverses the sidecar. Fix: bind 127.0.0.1, remove the debug exposure, and add a host firewall rule as defense in depth
The intentions are misconfigured; add a deny for the compromised container
The sidecar is broken; restart it
Enable intentions on the host network too
scenarios.why: Intentions and mTLS are properties of the sidecar path: traffic that never enters the proxy is never authenticated or authorized, by construction. No intention rule can govern a connection the mesh never sees — the 'deny the attacker' fix misunderstands the layer. The sidecar is healthy; the app routed around it. There is no 'intentions on the host network' — that is what host firewalls are for. The rule is absolute for sidecar deployments: the application listens on localhost, the sidecar owns the routable ports. Audit every service's bind address; 'for debugging' is how meshes get bypassed.
scenarios.hint: Which traffic do intentions and mesh mTLS actually govern?

scenarios.title: The allow that lost
scenarios.situation: Intentions: (1) deny * -> payments, (2) allow orders -> payments. Traffic from orders to payments is DENIED. The team reorders them in the UI; still denied. They conclude intentions are broken.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual precedence rule?
evidence: Exact: deny *-payments. Exact: allow orders-payments. UI order changed, no effect.
Consul evaluates most-specific match first; on equal specificity, DENY wins. UI ordering is cosmetic.
choices: Both intentions are equally specific (exact source+destination), so DENY wins regardless of order — the wildcard deny is not 'less specific' here because its destination is exact. Fix: remove or narrow the deny (e.g., deny specific unwanted sources) instead of fighting precedence; design intention sets so allows and denies do not collide at equal specificity
Intentions are evaluated top-down; put the allow first
The UI is buggy; use the API
Delete all intentions and start over
scenarios.why: Consul intention precedence is not firewall-rule ordering: specificity first, then deny-wins. A deny on *->payments and an allow on orders->payments tie on specificity (both name exact destinations), so deny prevails — no ordering tricks change that. The UI reorder was cargo-cult firewall thinking. Deleting everything is panic. The design lesson: avoid overlapping allow/deny at the same specificity; express 'default deny' as a single explicit default-deny plus targeted allows, not as a competing wildcard deny. When a deny must coexist with allows, make the deny MORE specific than the allows it should beat — or better, scope it to the actual unwanted sources.
scenarios.hint: How does Consul resolve conflicting intentions at equal specificity?

scenarios.title: The mesh trust cliff
scenarios.situation: The Connect CA (built-in) was created 2 years ago with default settings. Nobody rotated it. It expires in 30 days. 300 services rely on mesh mTLS.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rotation plan?
evidence: Consul built-in CA, expires in 30d. Leaf TTLs 72h, auto-rotated by sidecars.
CA expiry invalidates every leaf simultaneously — total mesh outage, not gradual degradation.
choices: Rotate the CA now with overlap: generate the new CA, distribute trust bundles containing BOTH CAs, let leaf rotation (72h TTL) roll the fleet onto the new chain, then retire the old CA — all before expiry. Then calendarize rotation (e.g., yearly) and alert at 90/60/30 days. Never let CA rotation become an emergency again
Increase leaf TTLs to reduce rotation churn during the event
Wait until expiry; the outage will be brief since leaves rotate fast
Switch to Vault PKI as CA during the emergency
scenarios.why: CA expiry is a cliff, not a slope: every leaf certificate chains to the CA, so expiry breaks all mTLS at once regardless of leaf TTLs. Longer leaf TTLs worsen the migration (slower rollover to the new chain). Waiting for expiry converts a planned rotation into a total outage. Switching CA providers mid-emergency adds migration risk to time pressure — change providers deliberately, not during a countdown. The correct pattern is overlap rotation: both CAs trusted during transition, leaves migrate via normal rotation, old CA retired after. And the meta-fix: CA expiry must be a monitored, calendarized, rehearsed event — it is the highest-leverage date in the mesh's life.
scenarios.hint: Why is CA expiry a cliff rather than gradual degradation?

scenarios.title: The legacy database
scenarios.situation: The mesh needs orders -> legacy-postgres (no sidecar possible; vendor appliance). The team opens the firewall 'temporarily' from every mesh node to the database.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Connect pattern?
evidence: Mesh service orders must reach non-mesh postgres. mTLS/intentions should still govern the call.
Host firewall opened mesh-wide to postgres: any compromised mesh node reaches the DB; no audit of which service connected.
choices: Terminating gateway: register legacy-postgres as an external service, route orders' traffic through a terminating gateway that originates the plaintext connection. Intentions (orders -> legacy-postgres) still authorize, and the firewall opens ONLY to the gateway hosts — the mesh's authorization extends to the legacy boundary instead of being punched through
The firewall rule is fine; add logging
Install a sidecar on the vendor appliance
Move the database into the mesh by force
scenarios.why: The firewall hole discards everything the mesh provides: no per-service authorization (any node, any service), no identity in the audit trail, and a blast radius of 'the whole mesh.' Logging the hole documents the bypass without closing it. Sidecars on vendor appliances are usually impossible (no shell, no agent). 'Move it into the mesh' ignores procurement reality. Terminating gateways exist for exactly this brownfield case: the mesh keeps its authorization model end-to-end, the gateway is the single audited egress point, and the firewall rule shrinks to gateway-hosts-only. It is also the migration path: when the legacy system is eventually meshed, only the gateway registration changes.
scenarios.hint: What is a terminating gateway for?

scenarios.title: The front door with no bouncer
scenarios.situation: External traffic hits the web service through an ingress gateway. The gateway routes to web, api, and admin services. There are no intentions on the gateway routes — 'the gateway authenticates with TLS.'
scenarios.prompt: What is missing?
evidence: Ingress Envoy terminates external TLS, routes by host/path to web, api, admin.
Gateway TLS is transport encryption, not authorization. No intentions defined for gateway -> service flows. admin is reachable externally.
choices: Authorization at the gateway: ingress gateways need intentions too — define which external identities (via JWT/OIDC claims or gateway service identity) may reach which services, and NEVER expose admin through the same gateway without explicit, audited intention. TLS at the edge proves the channel is encrypted, not that the caller is allowed
The gateway TLS is sufficient; add WAF rules
Remove the admin service from the gateway
Add mutual TLS for external clients
scenarios.why: Edge TLS answers 'is the pipe encrypted?' — it says nothing about 'should this caller reach admin?' Without intentions, the ingress gateway is a router, not a bouncer: anyone who reaches it can reach every backend it serves, including admin. WAF rules are a different layer (attack patterns, not identity authorization). Removing admin from this gateway is reasonable hardening but does not fix the missing authorization model for web/api. Client mTLS for external callers is heavy and still needs authorization policy on top. The mesh answer: intentions govern gateway-to-service flows like any mesh traffic — default deny, explicit allows, admin behind its own audited path or separate gateway.
scenarios.hint: What does edge TLS prove — and what does it NOT prove?

scenarios.title: The silent mesh
scenarios.situation: Orders calls payments; payments returns 503s. The app logs show timeouts. The mesh has no Envoy access logging enabled and no intention-deny metrics collected. Debugging is pure guesswork.
scenarios.prompt: What observability should the mesh have had?
evidence: 503s between services, app-level timeouts, no mesh telemetry.
Is it intentions? mTLS? Upstream down? Nobody can tell.
choices: Mesh-native telemetry: Envoy access logs (who called whom, response flags like UF/UC/UH that distinguish upstream failure from authz deny), intention-deny metrics (is the 503 actually a 403-in-disguise from intentions?), and cert-expiry/TLS-handshake metrics. The response flags alone usually name the layer: UF = upstream failure, UC = upstream connection termination — each flag maps to a troubleshooting runbook entry
Add more app-level logging and redeploy
Increase timeouts until the 503s stop
Restart the sidecars; Envoy occasionally wedges
scenarios.why: App logs see the symptom (timeout) but not the mesh layers that caused it — the sidecar sits between the app and the truth. More app logging cannot reveal intention denies or TLS failures; it just produces more timeout lines. Longer timeouts convert fast failures into slow ones. Restarting sidecars is hope-based operations. Envoy's access log response flags are the designed diagnostic: UF/URX/UH distinguish 'upstream dead' from 'no healthy upstream' from 'authz denied', and intention-deny counters confirm policy blocks. Enable access logging (sampled in high-traffic meshes), ship the flags to your logging stack, and write the flag-to-runbook mapping before the next incident.
scenarios.hint: What do Envoy response flags tell you that app timeouts cannot?

scenarios.title: The cross-DC call
scenarios.situation: dc1's orders needs dc2's fraud-check. The team opens firewall rules between datacenters and points orders at fraud-check's dc2 address directly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct federation pattern?
evidence: Cross-DC service call with mTLS and authorization preserved.
Direct firewall holes + hardcoded dc2 addresses: no intentions enforced cross-DC, addresses brittle, plaintext on the WAN unless separately arranged.
choices: Mesh gateways + WAN federation: federate the datacenters over WAN gossip, deploy mesh gateways in each DC, and let orders dial fraud-check through the local gateway — mTLS and intentions apply end-to-end, the WAN path is encrypted, and discovery stays dynamic instead of hardcoded
The firewall approach works; add TLS
Replicate fraud-check into dc1 to avoid cross-DC calls
Use a VPN between datacenters instead
scenarios.why: Direct firewall holes between datacenters recreate every problem the mesh solved, across the WAN: no service identity (IP-based rules), no intentions (authorization stops at the DC edge), brittle hardcoded addresses, and crypto as an afterthought. A VPN encrypts the pipe but provides no service-level authz. Replicating the service dodges the question (data residency, cost, and the next cross-DC call). Mesh gateways are the designed answer: federated trust, intentions enforced across DCs, encrypted WAN transit, and dynamic discovery — the mesh simply extends. The pattern to remember: wherever the mesh ends, its security properties end; extend the mesh instead of punching through it.
scenarios.hint: How do mesh security properties extend across datacenters?

scenarios.title: The plaintext backup
scenarios.situation: Daily Raft snapshots are stored unencrypted in a cloud bucket 'because the bucket is private.' The bucket logging shows a misconfigured IAM policy allowed public listing for 6 days last quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What is the severity and fix?
evidence: Daily, unencrypted, full Raft log = every secret in Vault, in one file.
Bucket listable publicly for 6 days; GetObject denied (mostly). Access logs incomplete.
choices: Critical: a snapshot IS the secrets database — treat it as secret material at the highest classification. Even list-only exposure is severe (object names leak metadata; any GetObject success is total compromise). Fix: encrypt snapshots before upload (age/gpg with keys in KMS/HSM), restrict bucket policy with explicit denies, enable object-level logging, and assume the exposed snapshots are compromised — rotate the crown-jewel secrets
Low severity; listing without GetObject is harmless
Move the bucket to private and continue unencrypted
Delete the old snapshots; the exposure window is closed
scenarios.why: A Raft snapshot contains every secret Vault holds — it is not 'a backup file,' it is the keys to the kingdom serialized. 'Private bucket' was the only control, and it failed; defense in depth demands encryption independent of bucket policy. List-only exposure still leaks object naming/metadata and you cannot prove no GetObject succeeded with incomplete logs — assume compromise of the exposed window. Deleting old snapshots does not un-expose them. The correct posture: encrypt-then-upload (so bucket policy is not the sole control), tight bucket policy with access logging, and a rotation plan for anything in the exposed snapshots. Backups of secrets are secrets.
scenarios.hint: What does a Raft snapshot contain, and what classification does that imply?

scenarios.title: The cron that died quietly
scenarios.situation: Snapshots run via cron on the Vault host. The cron broke 4 months ago when the host was rebuilt and nobody reinstalled it. Yesterday's ransomware incident needs a restore — the newest snapshot is 4 months old.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what is the systemic fix?
evidence: Newest snapshot 4 months old. RPO target was 24h. No monitoring on snapshot age.
Ransomware encrypted the Vault hosts; data recovery needs the snapshot. 4 months of secret rotations would be lost.
choices: Monitoring, not cron, failed: an unmonitored backup is not a backup. The systemic fix is snapshot-age alerting (alert if newest snapshot > RPO), snapshot jobs as managed automation (not host-local cron that dies with rebuilds), and restore drills that would have caught the gap months ago. For today: assess the 4-month-old snapshot vs. rebuilding from other sources (re-issuing dynamic creds is often faster than restoring stale statics)
Fix cron and move on; the incident is bad luck
Restore the 4-month snapshot immediately
Blame the host rebuild engineer
scenarios.why: Cron did not 'die quietly' — it died unobserved, which is the actual failure. Every backup system needs a freshness check that pages: 'newest snapshot older than RPO' is a tier-1 alert, as important as 'Vault sealed.' Host-local cron is fragile by nature; managed schedulers with centralized visibility survive rebuilds. And the quarterly restore drill exists precisely to catch this — a drill 3 months ago would have found the 3-month-old snapshot. For the immediate incident: restoring 4-month-old data loses 4 months of rotations (possibly worse than rebuilding), so evaluate both paths. Then implement the monitoring that makes 'quietly broken' impossible.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a backup job and a backup system?

scenarios.title: The premature promotion
scenarios.situation: The primary datacenter has network issues; the Vault primary is unreachable for 12 minutes. An engineer promotes the DR secondary 'to restore service.' Ten minutes later the primary's network recovers — now two clusters both believe they are primary.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong and how is it fixed?
evidence: Two primaries, divergent writes for 10 minutes (some secret rotations happened on each).
No declared-disaster criteria; promotion was a unilateral judgment call at 12 minutes of unreachability.
choices: Split-brain by procedure: promotion without a declared disaster and without fencing the old primary. Fix now: stop writes on one side immediately, determine which dataset is authoritative (or merge manually — there is no automatic merge), demote/rebuild the loser as a fresh secondary. Fix forever: written failover criteria (who declares, on what evidence, with what fencing of the old primary BEFORE promotion)
Keep both primaries; active-active is better anyway
Demote the original primary; the secondary is newer
Wait for replication to resolve the divergence
scenarios.why: Twelve minutes of unreachability is not a disaster — it is a network blip, and promoting on it created the real disaster: two writable primaries with divergent datasets. Replication does not 'resolve' divergence; DR replication is primary-to-secondary, and with two primaries there is no defined direction. 'Newer' is not 'authoritative' — both sides took valid writes. Active-active requires conflict resolution designed in advance, not declared after the fact. The procedural fix matters more than the technical one: failover needs a written decision process (declared disaster, evidence bar, old-primary fencing FIRST, then promote) executed by named humans — because the cost of wrong promotion exceeds the cost of waiting.
scenarios.hint: Why must the old primary be fenced BEFORE promoting the secondary?

scenarios.title: The drill that failed
scenarios.situation: The quarterly restore drill: fresh nodes, snapshot restore, unseal — fails at unseal. The Shamir key holders in the runbook: one left the company, one's share is on a dead laptop, and the third is on vacation. The drill is 3 hours in with no path forward.
scenarios.prompt: What does this failure actually prove?
evidence: Unseal ceremony: contact holders A, B, C. Reality: A departed, B's share lost, C unreachable.
14 months ago, by the departed holder A.
choices: The drill worked: it exposed that the unseal ceremony is broken BEFORE a real incident did. The failure is the finding. Fix: rekey immediately to invalidate lost shares, establish living key custody (current holders, verified shares, tested ceremony), consider auto-unseal to remove the human ceremony from the critical path, and put the ceremony itself on the drill schedule — unseal is part of DR, not separate from it
The drill was poorly planned; reschedule when C returns
Drills are disruptive; cancel them
Use the root token instead of unsealing
scenarios.why: A drill that fails has succeeded at its purpose: finding the break before the outage does. Rescheduling 'when everyone is available' optimizes for green drills, not for readiness — the incident will not wait for C's vacation to end. Canceling drills guarantees the next discovery happens at 3 AM. The root token cannot substitute for unseal (sealed Vault takes no requests, including root's). The real findings: key custody rotted (departed holders, dead laptops), the ceremony was never rehearsed, and 14 months without an unseal means nobody knew. Treat the drill failure as a P1 finding: rekey now, fix custody, automate where possible, and drill the ceremony quarterly — the drill IS the maintenance.
scenarios.hint: What does a failed DR drill prove?

scenarios.title: The restore that lied
scenarios.situation: The automated restore check is green: snapshot restores, Vault unseals, API responds. During a real incident, the restored cluster comes up — but the KV mount's data is from 6 months ago. The check never read any actual secret.
scenarios.prompt: What was missing from verification?
evidence: Restore -> unseal -> /sys/health 200 -> GREEN. No data validation.

Snapshot job had been snapshotting a STANDBY node whose Raft log lagged due to a network issue — snapshots were stale for 6 months. Health checks passed because the node was healthy; the DATA was old.
choices: Content verification: canary secrets. The check validated liveness (process up, API responding) but never freshness or completeness. Fix: write known canary values to every backend, have the restore check READ them and assert values AND recency (canary rotated daily — if the canary is old, the snapshot is old). Alert on canary age, not just restore success
The check is fine; stale snapshots are unavoidable
Snapshot the active node instead; problem solved
Increase snapshot frequency
scenarios.why: Health checks answer 'is it up?' — they cannot answer 'is the data right?' A restore verification that never reads data verifies the container, not the backup. Snapshotting a lagging standby is a real failure mode (standbys can lag; the snapshot faithfully captured stale state), and only content checks catch it. Snapshotting the active instead is reasonable hardening but does not replace verification — the active could have its own issues. More frequent snapshots of stale data just produce fresher-looking staleness. Canaries close the loop: a daily-rotated canary makes staleness self-evident (yesterday's canary value in today's restore = 24h+ stale). Verify content, not just liveness — for backups above all.
scenarios.hint: Why is /sys/health 200 insufficient as restore verification?

scenarios.title: The CA compromise fire drill
scenarios.situation: Game day scenario: the PKI intermediate key is suspected compromised. The runbook says 'rotate the CA.' The team discovers: no documented chain inventory (which services use which intermediate?), no client trust-bundle distribution mechanism, and leaf TTLs of 90 days (rotation will take months to propagate).
scenarios.prompt: What must the CA-compromise runbook contain?
evidence: No chain inventory, no trust-bundle pipeline, 90-day leaf TTLs, no rehearsal ever.
Suspected compromise = active incident; every hour of delay is attacker minting time.
choices: A CA-compromise runbook needs: (1) chain inventory (which intermediates sign what, which clients trust which bundles) — built BEFORE the incident; (2) a trust-bundle distribution pipeline (config management push to all clients); (3) short leaf TTLs normally (so fleet rollover is days, not months); (4) the rotation sequence (new intermediate -> distribute bundle with both -> flip issuance -> revoke old -> monitor); (5) a rehearsal record. Today's 90-day TTLs mean the team must ALSO do emergency leaf reissuance for critical services while the fleet rolls
Just revoke the intermediate; clients will error visibly and can be fixed
Rotate the root too, to be safe
Wait for confirmed (not suspected) compromise before acting
scenarios.why: Revoking without a distribution plan breaks every client simultaneously — 'visible errors' across the fleet is an outage, not a response. Rotating the root as well doubles the work under fire for no benefit (the root was not compromised; the offline root is the anchor you rotate TO). Waiting for confirmation gives the attacker the confirmation window to mint at leisure — suspected CA compromise is treated as real until proven otherwise. The hard truth this drill exposes: CA-compromise response is 90% preparation (inventory, distribution pipeline, short TTLs, rehearsals) and 10% execution. You cannot build the inventory during the incident. Write the runbook now, rehearse it yearly, and fix the 90-day leaf TTLs regardless — they make EVERY rotation an emergency.
scenarios.hint: What are the five components of a CA-compromise runbook?

scenarios.title: The backup in the same building
scenarios.situation: All Vault snapshots live on a NAS in the same datacenter as the cluster. The DR plan says 'restore from NAS.' A facilities incident (flooding) takes out the datacenter.
scenarios.prompt: What is the DR gap?
evidence: NAS in building A, same as the cluster. No off-site copies.
'Restore from NAS' — assumes the building survives.
choices: The backup shares the fate of the primary: any site-level event (flood, fire, extended power loss) destroys both the cluster AND its backups. The fix is the 3-2-1 rule applied for real: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 off-site (different region/facility) — encrypted snapshots replicated to object storage in another region, with restore tested FROM the off-site copy, not just the local NAS
Buy a better NAS with RAID
The flood is unlikely; accept the risk formally
Move the NAS to the floor above
scenarios.why: RAID protects against disk failure, not building failure — a better NAS in the same flood zone is the same risk with better specs. Risk acceptance is legitimate only when it is explicit, priced, and signed — 'unlikely' is not analysis. A different floor is the same building. The 3-2-1 rule exists because correlated failures are the ones that kill you: the events most likely to require a restore (site loss) are exactly the events that destroy co-located backups. Off-site means a different failure domain (region, not rack), encrypted in transit and at rest, with the restore drill executed from the off-site copy at least yearly — because a backup you have never restored from off-site is a theory.
scenarios.hint: What does the 3-2-1 rule protect against that RAID does not?

lessons.title: Secrets Engines — Core concepts
concepts: KV engine: the database engine generates per-client dynamic credentials (CREATE ROLE with TTL), so there's no shared password to rotate in lockstep — each lease simply expires and the service fetches a fresh one.

kv-v2 versioning: this is why kv-v2 is the default choice for human-managed secrets, with check-and-set (CAS) for safe concurrent writes. Policies match the real API paths, so kv-v2 policies must use secret/data/...

lessons.title: Auth Methods — Core concepts
concepts: AppRole is designed for machines: role_id is non-secret identity, secret_id is the secret credential — delivered separately (ideally via different channels).

Machine auth: the initial root token is a bootstrap credential: log in, configure real auth (OIDC/LDAP), write least-privilege policies, then 'vault token revoke' the root token. Humans should auth via the company IdP: LDAP (bind + group mapping) or OIDC (SSO with group claims mapped to policies via groups/roles).

Kubernetes auth: the K8s auth method: Vault is configured with the cluster's API endpoint and CA; the Pod presents its service-account token (JWT); Vault verifies it with the K8s TokenReview API and checks it against role bindings (bound_service_account_names, bound_service_account_namespaces).
Service tokens are the persistent, renewable default for interactive/long-lived use.

Tokens: bound CIDRs, secret_id TTLs, and per-role policies scope it tightly. userpass is for humans; hardcoded tokens are the anti-pattern. Batch tokens are encrypted blobs (not stored server-side): cheap to create at massive scale, ideal for ephemeral high-volume use.

concepts: Policy syntax: in Vault policy evaluation, an explicit deny on a path overrides all allows — it's the carve-out mechanism. The 'default' policy (attached to every token unless explicitly excluded) allows a token to look itself up, renew itself, and use its cubbyhole.

lessons.title: Consul Service Mesh — Core concepts
concepts: Raft quorum: consul servers maintain the catalog via Raft consensus — quorum needs 2n+1 (3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2). But values are stored unencrypted and replicated in Raft logs — it's not a secret manager.
Service discovery: consul serves DNS on port 8600 (service.consul domain: <service>.service.consul, with tag/datacenter variants) and a rich HTTP API (/v1/catalog, /v1/health).
DNS is the zero-code path; the API gives metadata, tags, and Connect info.

Health checks (script/http/tcp/TTL/docker) should test the service itself cheaply — a deep check coupling to downstream deps causes cascading flaps. Clients are lightweight agents on every node: they run health checks, gossip membership via Serf (fast failure detection), and forward requests to servers.
Flapping usually means the check is too strict or too deep.

lessons.title: Operations — Core concepts
concepts: Shamir's Secret Sharing splits the key: any threshold (3 of 5) reconstructs it.

Raft storage: integrated Raft storage is the recommended backend: Vault nodes replicate via Raft directly (3 or 5 nodes for quorum), snapshots via 'vault operator raft snapshot save/restore'. Rolling upgrade: standby nodes first (they rejoin and catch up via Raft), then failover the active (step-down) and upgrade it.

HA: audit devices record authenticated requests and responses (sensitive fields HMAC'd, not plaintext) — the compliance trail for 'who accessed what'. Raft snapshots are the DR mechanism: scheduled 'snapshot save' (keep them encrypted/offsite — they contain everything), restore onto fresh nodes.
Backup: test restores periodically; an untested backup is a hope. Like Vault: replication ≠ backup; test the restore path before you need it.
Raft snapshots: consul snapshot save captures the Raft state atomically (any server works — the request forwards to the leader).
