lessons.title: Vault & Consul — Core concepts
concepts: Vault is a secrets manager, not a config store: the KV engine holds static secrets, while dynamic engines (database, PKI, AWS) mint short-lived credentials that expire instead of needing rotation.
Every Vault request is authenticated (token, AppRole, JWT/OIDC, Kubernetes auth) and then authorized by policies — capabilities are per-path, so design least-privilege policies before issuing tokens.
Vault seals protect data at rest: Shamir key shares split trust among humans, while auto-unseal via KMS/HSM lets clusters recover from restarts without 3 AM key ceremonies.
Consul provides service discovery with health checks — the catalog and DNS only advertise passing instances, turning failover from a manual task into an automatic one.
Consul Connect adds a service mesh: sidecar proxies enforce mutual TLS for identity, and intentions declare which services are allowed to communicate.
Consul's KV store is for configuration, not secrets — it lacks Vault's encryption, audit, and lease semantics, so never store credentials there.

example.code:
vault kv put secret/app/db password="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"
vault policy write app-read - <<'EOF'
path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF
example.walkthrough: The first command writes a generated password into the KV engine. The heredoc defines a policy allowing read-only access under secret/data/app/* (note the /data/ infix for KV v2). Tokens minted against this policy can read app secrets and nothing else.

pitfalls: Common trap: using a root token for automation — root bypasses all policies; mint least-privilege tokens via auth methods instead.
Common trap: treating Consul KV as a secrets store — it is plaintext config distribution without Vault's protections.
Common trap: long-lived static credentials in KV that nobody rotates — prefer dynamic secrets with TTLs.
Common trap: confusing gossip encryption with service-mesh mTLS — gossip encryption protects Consul's chatter, not your application traffic.

lessons.title: KV Engine Deep Dive: v1 vs v2 Operations
concepts: kv-v2 versions every write and keeps max-versions history; delete is soft (undelete restores), destroy is permanent, and metadata/ tracks versions independently of data/.

Policy paths differ: kv-v2 requires secret/data/app for reads, secret/metadata/app for version management, secret/destroy/app and secret/undelete/app for lifecycle — the number-one policy bug is writing kv-v1 paths against a v2 mount.
Check-and-set (CAS): pass cas=<version> on write to make concurrent writers safe; a stale CAS fails instead of silently overwriting.
Tune per mount: max-versions, cas-required, delete-version-after. Set delete-version-after for compliance auto-expiry of old versions.

example.code:
vault kv put -mount=secret app/db password=s3cret
vault kv get -version=2 -mount=secret app/db
# policy needs: secret/data/app/db (read), secret/metadata/app/db (list)
example.walkthrough: kv-v2 policies copied from kv-v1 examples fail closed with 'permission denied' — always include the /data/ path.

pitfalls: Enabling kv-v2 on an existing v1 mount path without migrating data expectations — versioning changes delete semantics.
Granting secret/app/* instead of secret/data/app/*: looks right, denies everything on v2.
Ignoring max-versions: unbounded history grows storage and leaks old secrets past rotation.

lessons.title: Cubbyhole and Response Wrapping
concepts: Cubbyhole is a per-token KV that dies with the token: perfect for bootstrapping (drop the AppRole secret-id in cubbyhole, hand the wrapping token to the app).
Response wrapping: Vault returns a single-use wrapping token instead of the secret; the recipient unwraps within the TTL. The secret never sits in logs, CI output, or chat.
Wrapping works on any response: vault kv get -wrap-ttl=60s, or wrap an AppRole secret-id. TTLs are short (minutes) — wrapping is a delivery mechanism, not storage.
Audit still records that a wrap happened (request path, no secret bytes) — you get delivery proof without secret exposure.

example.code:
vault kv get -wrap-ttl=120 -mount=secret app/db   # returns wrapping_token, not the secret
vault unwrap <wrapping_token>                      # single use, then it is gone
example.walkthrough: Wrap a KV read, then unwrap it; observe the audit log shows the wrap but not the value.

pitfalls: Wrapping with a 24h TTL: long-lived wrapping tokens are just secrets with extra steps.
Unwrapping twice: the token is single-use; the second unwrap fails and the secret must be re-wrapped.
Using cubbyhole for durable storage: it evaporates with the token — it is a mailbox, not a vault.
lessons.try_it: Deliver a secret to a teammate using only a wrapping token; verify they cannot unwrap twice.

lessons.title: Lease Mechanics and Revocation
concepts: Every dynamic secret and service token carries a lease: TTL, max TTL, renewable flag. Expiry is enforced server-side; clients must renew or re-request.
Renewal: vault lease renew extends within max TTL. Apps should renew at ~2/3 of TTL and handle renewal failure by re-authenticating — the standard agent/sidecar pattern.
Revocation: vault lease revoke kills one lease; revoke-prefix kills a subtree (e.g., all creds from database/creds/). Revocation is the incident-response kill switch.
Lease storms: thousands of clients renewing on the same schedule thundering-herd the leader. Jitter renewal and stagger TTLs.

example.code:
vault lease renew database/creds/orders-role/abc123
vault lease revoke -prefix=database/creds/orders-role   # kill switch
example.walkthrough: Revoke a lease prefix and watch the app fail closed; then fix the app to re-request on 403.

pitfalls: Setting TTLs longer than the rotation policy requires: the lease IS the rotation interval.
Non-renewable tokens for long-lived services: they expire and the 3 AM page is yours.
revoke-prefix typos: a wrong prefix revokes the wrong subtree — dry-run with lease lookup first.
lessons.try_it: Issue a 5-minute dynamic credential, renew it once, then revoke-prefix and observe.

lessons.title: Mount Tuning and Engine Options
concepts: vault secrets tune sets per-mount default TTL, max TTL, and listing visibility; tune the mount, not every role, so policy stays DRY.
default-lease-ttl and max-lease-ttl on the mount bound every credential issued there — the mount is the guardrail, roles are the refinement.
Move and remount: vault secrets move relocates a mount's data to a new path; plan path layouts (secret/, transit/, pki/) before production data lands.
Disable with care: vault secrets disable destroys the mount AND its data. There is no undo — snapshot first, every time.

example.code:
vault secrets tune -default-lease-ttl=1h -max-lease-ttl=24h secret/
vault secrets move secret/ secret-v1-archived/
example.walkthrough: Tune a mount's TTLs, issue a credential, and confirm the lease honors the mount bounds.

pitfalls: Tuning max-lease-ttl DOWN on a mount with outstanding long leases: existing leases keep old TTLs, new ones clamp — know which you are testing.
Disabling a mount to 'clean up' in prod: data loss. Snapshot, verify, then disable.
Forgetting listing-visibility: tune it so UIs do not leak mount names to low-privilege tokens.
lessons.try_it: Snapshot, then practice a secrets move on a scratch mount.

lessons.title: Token Auth: Service Tokens vs Batch Tokens
concepts: Service tokens are the heavyweight default: renewable, revocable individually, carry leases, and appear in the token store. Use for long-lived, important identities.
Batch tokens are lightweight: no storage, non-renewable, fixed short TTL, ideal for high-volume ephemeral use (sidecar injection at scale). They cannot be revoked individually — only by expiry.
Token hierarchy: parent tokens can revoke children; orphan tokens break the chain. Use orphan sparingly — hierarchy is your blast-radius control.
Periodic tokens (period set) renew indefinitely without a max TTL — the right shape for agents/daemons; guard them with tight policies and CIDR bounds.

example.code:
vault token create -policy=orders -ttl=1h -renewable=true
vault token create -type=batch -ttl=5m   # high-volume, ephemeral
example.walkthrough: Create both token types; revoke the parent of a service token and watch the child die.

pitfalls: Handing out periodic tokens with broad policies: infinite lifetime + broad access is a standing breach.
Using batch tokens where revocation matters: you cannot kill one — only wait for expiry.
Orphan tokens everywhere: you lose the ability to revoke whole subtrees on incident.
lessons.try_it: Build a token hierarchy three deep, revoke the middle, verify the cascade.

lessons.title: AppRole: The Machine Auth Workhorse
concepts: AppRole splits identity into role-id (public, like a username) and secret-id (secret, like a password) — machines authenticate without human credentials baked into images.
Harden it: bind secret-id to CIDR, set secret-id TTL and num_uses, rotate via secret-id destruction. A leaked role-id alone grants nothing.
Response-wrap the secret-id delivery: the orchestrator wraps it, the app unwraps at boot. The secret-id never lands in config files or env dumps.
Token tuning on the role: token_ttl, token_max_ttl, token_policies, token_bound_cidrs. The role defines the blast radius of every login it issues.

example.code:
vault write auth/approle/role/orders token_policies=orders \
  secret_id_num_uses=1 secret_id_ttl=10m token_ttl=1h
vault write -f auth/approle/role/orders/secret-id -wrap-ttl=60s
example.walkthrough: Stand up AppRole for a demo service with CIDR-bound, single-use secret-ids.

pitfalls: Single static secret-id checked into the repo: you have recreated the password-in-git problem.
No CIDR binding: a stolen secret-id is usable from anywhere.
token_ttl of 30 days on a machine role: machines should re-authenticate hourly, not monthly.
lessons.try_it: Steal your own secret-id from another IP and confirm the CIDR bind rejects it.

lessons.title: Kubernetes and Cloud Auth Methods
concepts: Kubernetes auth: Vault trusts the cluster's service-account JWTs; a pod authenticates with its projected token, bound to serviceaccount name and namespace. No static credentials in the cluster.
Cloud auth (AWS/GCP/Azure): Vault validates instance identity documents (PKCS7, signed metadata) or IAM ARNs. The cloud IS the credential — nothing to distribute.
Bound parameters are the security: bound_service_account_namespaces, bound_iam_principal_arn. Loose bounds ('any pod in the cluster') collapse the method to theater.
Rotation story: projected K8s tokens auto-rotate; Vault re-validates each login. Short token TTLs (minutes to an hour) keep the window tight.

example.code:
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/orders \
  bound_service_account_names=orders-sa \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=("prod") \
  policies=orders ttl=1h
example.walkthrough: Configure K8s auth for a namespace and log in from a pod using its projected token.

pitfalls: bound_service_account_names='*' to 'make it work': any compromised pod can now mint tokens.
Caching the Vault token in a Secret object: you have laundered a short-lived credential into a long-lived one.
Skipping audience binding: tokens minted for other audiences may be replayable.
lessons.try_it: Attempt login from a pod in the wrong namespace; verify denial.

lessons.title: Userpass, LDAP, and OIDC
concepts: Userpass is the bootstrap method: fine for break-glass admins and small teams, terrible at scale — no MFA, no central deprovisioning. Enable, create admins, then move humans to OIDC/LDAP.
LDAP auth delegates to directory: Vault binds, searches, and maps groups to policies via group aliases. Deprovisioning happens in the directory, not in Vault — that is the point.
OIDC is the modern human path: SSO with MFA enforced by the IdP, group claims mapped to policies. Configure bound_claims and claim_mappings; verify group membership actually restricts.
Auth method priority for interviews: humans → OIDC; machines on K8s → K8s auth; machines off K8s → AppRole; cloud VMs → cloud auth; break-glass → userpass.

example.code:
vault write auth/oidc/role/engineers bound_audiences=CLIENT_ID \
  allowed_redirect_uris=https://vault.example.com/ui/vault/auth/oidc/oidc/callback \
  policies=engineers oidc_scopes=email,groups
example.walkthrough: Map an OIDC group claim to a policy and log in to prove the mapping.

pitfalls: Leaving userpass enabled with weak passwords after OIDC is live: it becomes the bypass around your SSO+MFA.
LDAP group alias mis-mapping: users authenticate but land with zero policies — test with a real login.
OIDC without bound_claims: any valid IdP user gets the role's policies.
lessons.try_it: Audit enabled auth methods; disable or restrict any that bypass your SSO.

lessons.title: Auth Method Tuning and MFA
concepts: Tune per method: default TTL, max TTL, token type, listing visibility. A 30-day userpass token defeats the purpose of short-lived service credentials.
MFA enforcement: configure MFA methods (TOTP, Okta, Duo, PingID) and attach enforcement to mounts, namespaces, or identities — MFA on the admin paths, not just the login.
Step-up auth: require MFA only for sensitive operations (unseal-adjacent paths, root-adjacent mounts). Blanket MFA everywhere trains users to approve blindly.
Identity entities and aliases: one human, many auth methods, one entity — policies attach to the entity so access survives method changes.

example.code:
vault write identity/mfa/login-enforcement/admin-paths \
  mfa_method_ids=tOTP-method auth_method_types=userpass \
  identity_group_ids=admins-group
example.walkthrough: Enforce TOTP on the break-glass userpass method and test the login flow.

pitfalls: MFA on every path: alert fatigue applies to push approvals too — scope it to privileged actions.
Policies on aliases instead of entities: switching a user from LDAP to OIDC silently drops their access.
No MFA on break-glass: the highest-privilege path with the weakest auth is the attacker's first target.
lessons.try_it: Draw your identity map: every human, their methods, their entity, their MFA coverage.

lessons.title: Policy Syntax and Path Matching
concepts: Policies are deny-by-default: no policy grants means no access, even for authenticated tokens. Every grant must be explicit.
Path matching: 'secret/data/app/*' matches one level; 'secret/data/app/+' is the single-segment wildcard. Trailing /* does not cross segment boundaries the way newcomers expect.
Capabilities: create, read, update, delete, list, sudo. Minimal viable: read+list for consumers; update without delete for writers who should not destroy.
Write policies as files, store in git, apply via vault policy write. Click-ops policies are unreviewable and unrepeatable.

example.walkthrough: Write a least-privilege policy for a service from scratch, apply it, and test every path with a token.

pitfalls: Granting 'secret/*' to 'keep it simple': one typo'd application path away from total secret access.
Forgetting list on metadata: the UI and CLI list calls fail and users blame Vault instead of the policy.
sudo capability on broad paths: sudo bypasses some guards — scope it to named admin paths only.
lessons.try_it: Take a broad policy you wrote and cut it to minimal capabilities; verify the app still works.

lessons.title: ACL Capabilities in Practice
concepts: Map capabilities to intent: read (get values), list (browse keys), create/update (write values), delete (soft-delete v2), plus destroy/undelete via their dedicated paths.
Deny clauses: explicit 'deny' stanzas override allows — use for carve-outs (allow secret/data/* except secret/data/prod/root).
Parameter constraints: allowed_parameters / denied_parameters restrict WHICH fields a writer can set (e.g., force ttl values on PKI roles).
Test like code: vault token capabilities <token> <path> shows the effective grant. Run it before handing the token to the app team.

example.walkthrough: Constrain a PKI role policy so it can only issue for one domain suffix.

pitfalls: allowed_parameters on the wrong path: the constraint silently never applies — test with a violating request.
Assuming update implies create: some paths require explicit create; test both verbs.
No deny carve-outs on shared mounts: one team's 'convenient' policy becomes everyone's over-grant.
lessons.try_it: Use token capabilities to audit three existing tokens; document over-grants.

lessons.title: Policy Templates and Templated ACLs
concepts: Templated ACLs inject identity metadata into paths: secret/data/{{identity.entity.name}}/* gives each human their own cubby without writing N policies.
Available template params: identity.entity.id, identity.entity.name, identity.entity.metadata.*, identity.groups.ids. Metadata set at entity creation drives the rest.
Pattern: one 'self-service' policy with templated paths attached to all human entities; team policies attached via group membership.
Templates fail closed: if the metadata key is missing, the path does not match — which reads as a confusing deny. Validate metadata exists for every entity.

example.walkthrough: Build a templated self-service policy and verify two users land in different paths.

pitfalls: Templating on a metadata key you never populate: every user gets denied and the policy 'looks right'.
Over-broad templates: {{identity.entity.name}}/* under secret/data/shared/ is a sharing violation.
Forgetting that group ids (not names) go in templates — names are not stable identifiers.
lessons.try_it: Add a metadata field to your entity and reference it in a templated path.

lessons.title: Sentinel and EGP/RGP Basics
concepts: Sentinel policies are code that runs on the request path: endpoint-governing policies (EGP) on API endpoints, role-governing policies (RGP) on roles. Deny-by-exception logic lives here.
Use cases: business-hours-only unseal-adjacent operations, CIDR + MFA combined conditions, blocking secret writes containing known-bad patterns, requiring JIRA ticket IDs in request metadata.
Sentinel is the 'policy about policy': when ACL capabilities are too coarse (they cannot say 'only on Tuesdays'), Sentinel evaluates the when.
Keep Sentinel small and tested: every Sentinel rule is code in the request path — a buggy rule denies production traffic. Test with sentinel test before deploying.

example.walkthrough: Write a Sentinel rule that blocks writes outside business hours; test it in dry-run.

pitfalls: Sentinel as a substitute for ACLs: it is slower and harder to audit — ACLs first, Sentinel for what ACLs cannot express.
Untested Sentinel in prod: one bad import and every request to the endpoint fails closed.
No logging on Sentinel denies: operators cannot distinguish 'policy said no' from 'Vault is broken.'
lessons.try_it: List three access rules in your org that ACLs cannot express; draft one as Sentinel.

lessons.title: Policy Debugging: Why Access Was Denied
concepts: Debug ladder: (1) vault token lookup — is the token valid, what policies attach? (2) vault policy read — does the path match, are capabilities right? (3) audit log — what path did the request ACTUALLY hit?
The classic: kv-v2 request to secret/app/db hits secret/data/app/db. The audit log shows the real path; the policy author guessed the logical one.
token capabilities is the fastest oracle: it evaluates the merged policy set against a path without making the request.
Namespace gotcha: policies are namespace-local; a policy that works in ns1/ silently does nothing when the token is used in ns2/.

example.code:
vault token lookup | grep policies
vault token capabilities $TOKEN secret/data/app/db
# then compare against the audit log's actual request path
example.walkthrough: Break a policy on purpose, then debug it using only the ladder — no guessing.

pitfalls: Editing the policy file but forgetting vault policy write: the running policy is the old one.
Debugging the app instead of the token: always reproduce with curl/CLI and the raw token first.
Multiple overlapping policies: the union applies — read ALL attached policies, not just the one you wrote.
lessons.try_it: Document your team's policy-debug ladder in the runbook.

lessons.title: Database Engine: Roles and Rotation
concepts: The database engine holds ONE privileged root credential and mints per-client credentials via CREATE ROLE / DROP ROLE SQL — clients never share a password.
Two role types: dynamic (fresh creds per lease, auto-revoked) and static (rotates the stored password on a schedule for apps that cannot do dynamic).
Root rotation: vault write -f database/rotate-root/<name> rotates the privileged credential Vault itself uses — rotate it on schedule, not just at setup.
Tune creation_statements per least privilege: the minted role should own exactly what the app needs, nothing more.

example.code:
vault write database/config/prod db_plugin=postgresql \
  connection_url='postgresql://{{username}}:{{password}}@db:5432/app'
vault write database/roles/orders db_name=prod \
  creation_statements='CREATE ROLE...' default_ttl=1h
example.walkthrough: Configure the DB engine against a scratch Postgres and mint a dynamic credential.

pitfalls: Static root password in the config that never rotates: Vault becomes a password museum.
Over-privileged creation_statements: every minted credential inherits the excess — SUPERUSER templates are a breach waiting.
Forgetting rotate-root: the one credential that can mint all others is the stalest.
lessons.try_it: Rotate the root credential and confirm existing leases keep working.

lessons.title: AWS, GCP, and Azure Dynamic Credentials
concepts: Cloud engines mint short-lived IAM credentials: AWS STS tokens or IAM users, GCP service-account keys or OAuth tokens, Azure service principals — scoped by the role you define.
AWS role types: iam_user (Vault creates/deletes users), assumed_role (STS AssumeRole — no IAM users created, cleaner), federation_token. Prefer assumed_role where possible.
Credential types map to TTL thinking: STS creds live minutes-to-hours; IAM users persist until revoked. Match the type to the job length.
The Vault server needs its own cloud credential to mint others — bootstrap with instance roles/IRSA, never a static access key in config.

example.code:
vault write aws/roles/deployer credential_type=assumed_role \
  role_arns=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deployer ttl=1h
example.walkthrough: Mint an STS credential via Vault and use it for one AWS CLI call; watch it expire.

pitfalls: Static AWS keys in Vault server config: the minter's credential outlives everything it mints.
iam_user roles at scale: orphaned IAM users accumulate — audit and prefer STS.
Wildcard policies on the role: the minted credential's power equals the role's policy — scope it.
lessons.try_it: List credentials Vault has minted this week; revoke the stale ones.

lessons.title: SSH Secrets Engine: OTP and Signed Keys
concepts: Three modes: OTP (one-time password per login, verified against Vault), dynamic keys (Vault generates a keypair per session), signed keys (Vault CA signs the user's public key — hosts trust the CA, not key lists).
Signed SSH certificates are the scalable answer: hosts carry one trusted CA line; users get short-lived certs with principals. No more authorized_keys sprawl.
OTP mode needs the vault-ssh-helper on the host to verify the OTP with Vault — it is a per-host agent, best for small fleets or break-glass.
Key IDs and principals: bake identity into the cert (key_id=user, principals=user,role). The SSH log then shows WHO, not just which key.

example.code:
vault write ssh-client-signer/sign/web -format=json public_key=@$HOME/.ssh/id_rsa.pub \
  | jq -r .data.signed_key > ~/.ssh/id_rsa-cert.pub
example.walkthrough: Set up the SSH CA, sign your key, and SSH with the certificate.

pitfalls: OTP helper misconfigured: logins fail with no useful error — test the helper's Vault connectivity first.
Signing certs with 52-week TTLs: you have recreated static keys with extra steps. Hours, not months.
Forgetting principals: a cert with no principals authenticates as nobody useful.
lessons.try_it: Expire a cert and confirm the host rejects it; that is your revocation story.

lessons.title: Lease Lifecycle: Renew, Revoke, Rollback
concepts: Renewal pattern: renew at 2/3 TTL; on renewal failure, re-authenticate and re-request. Bake this into every client — the Vault Agent does it for you; hand-rolled clients must implement it.
Revoke is the kill switch: single lease, prefix, or all. Incident runbook step one is revoke-prefix on the compromised role's leases.
Rollback safety: when rotating a database password, keep the old credential valid until all clients have picked up the new one — dual-password windows prevent self-inflicted outages.
Monitor lease counts: a climbing lease count with flat traffic means clients are minting without revoking — a slow leak toward storage exhaustion.

example.code:
# client loop: renew at 2/3 TTL, re-auth on failure
vault lease renew -increment=3600 <lease-id> || re_authenticate
example.walkthrough: Write a client loop that renews, and test the re-auth path by revoking mid-run.

pitfalls: No renewal logic: the app works until the first TTL expiry, then pages you at 3 AM.
revoke without a re-request path: you have built a denial-of-service button for yourself.
Ignoring lease-count metrics: the leak is silent until the storage backend fills.
lessons.try_it: Graph lease counts for a week; set an alert on abnormal growth.

lessons.title: Static Roles vs Dynamic Roles
concepts: Static roles rotate a STORED credential on a schedule (rotation_period): for legacy apps that can only read one password from one place. The app re-reads; Vault handles the change.
Dynamic roles mint FRESH credentials per request: for apps you control. No coordination, no shared secret, automatic revocation.
Decision rule: can the app handle credential churn? Yes → dynamic. No (hardcoded single password, no reload) → static role with rotation.
Static rotation has a hazard window: during rotation, old and new overlap — configure rotation_schedule and verify the app tolerates both briefly.

example.code:
vault write database/static-roles/legacy-app db_name=prod \
  username=legacy_app rotation_period=24h
example.walkthrough: Stand up a static role for a fake legacy app; rotate and verify continuity.

pitfalls: Static roles for everything 'because it is simpler': you keep the shared-secret coordination problem Vault was bought to kill.
rotation_period shorter than the app's re-read interval: the app reads the password Vault already replaced.
No monitoring on rotation failures: a failed rotation leaves the stored password stale silently.
lessons.try_it: Migrate one static-role consumer toward dynamic creds; document what blocked it.

lessons.title: Service Discovery: Catalog, Health, DNS
concepts: The catalog is Consul's source of truth: every service registration, node, and health-check result. The agent on each node feeds it; servers replicate via Raft.
Health checks drive everything: a failing check removes the instance from DNS and API results automatically. Checks are the load balancer's brain.
DNS interface: <service>.service.consul resolves to healthy instances only. SRV records expose ports. No client libraries needed — any DNS resolver works.
Anti-entropy: agents continuously reconcile local state with the catalog. A manually edited service file gets corrected — the catalog wins.

example.code:
dig @127.0.0.1 -p 8600 orders.service.consul
# only healthy instances answer; failing ones vanish automatically
example.walkthrough: Register a service with a health check, break the check, and watch DNS stop returning it.

pitfalls: Health checks that always pass: discovery lies and traffic hits dead instances.
Querying the catalog instead of DNS/API for 'all' instances: you bypass health filtering.
TTL-based external checks with no deregistration: flapping services churn the catalog.
lessons.try_it: Add a deregister_critical_service_after to every check you own.

lessons.title: KV Store and Sessions
concepts: Consul KV is a datacenter-local configuration store: feature flags, service config, leader-election locks. It is not a secrets store — no encryption at rest by default.
Sessions tie KV keys to health: a lock acquired with a session releases automatically when the session's health check fails. This is distributed locking done right.
CAS operations on KV (ModifyIndex) give optimistic concurrency: read-modify-write without a lock for low-contention keys.
Long-poll with ?index=: blocking queries turn KV into a config-distribution channel — consul-template watches and rewrites app config on change.

example.code: consul lock -name=deploy/web ./deploy.sh   # session-backed distributed lock
example.walkthrough: Use consul lock to serialize a deploy across three shells; kill one holder and watch the lock release.

pitfalls: Storing secrets in KV: it is plaintext gossip-adjacent — use Vault, reference from KV.
Locks without sessions: a crashed holder keeps the lock forever.
Blocking queries without index handling: busy-loop polling hammers the servers.
lessons.try_it: Implement leader election for a cron job using a KV lock with sessions.

lessons.title: Gossip Protocol and Agent Roles
concepts: Gossip (Serf, UDP) is the failure detector: agents probe each other randomly, spreading membership and failure news in O(log n) time. This is how Consul knows a node died.
Server agents form the Raft quorum and hold the catalog; client agents are the local cache and forwarder on every node. Apps talk to the local client — never directly to servers.
Gossip encryption (encrypt key in config): without it, membership traffic is plaintext and joinable by anyone. Generate with consul keygen, distribute securely.
LAN gossip vs WAN gossip: datacenters federate over WAN gossip; service discovery stays datacenter-local by default, failover is explicit.

example.code:
consul keygen   # 32-byte gossip encryption key
# agent config: { "encrypt": "<key>", "server": true, "bootstrap_expect": 3 }
example.walkthrough: Form a 3-server cluster with gossip encryption; capture traffic and confirm it is opaque.

pitfalls: Clients talking to servers directly: you lose caching and add Raft load — always via local client.
bootstrap_expect wrong: 1 in prod risks split-brain; 3+ with only 2 nodes never elects.
No gossip encryption: anyone on the network can join the gossip pool and lie about membership.
lessons.try_it: Verify every agent config in your fleet carries the encrypt key.

lessons.title: Prepared Queries and Service Router
concepts: Prepared queries are stored discovery templates: name, service, tags, datacenter failover, nearest-routing. Apps query one name; Consul resolves the topology.
Failover: a prepared query can list remote datacenters in order — when local has zero healthy instances, DNS/API transparently returns the remote set.
Nearest routing: with network coordinates, queries return instances sorted by network round-trip — latency-aware discovery without a smart client.
Service router (Connect): L7 routing by path/header on top of discovery — the mesh's traffic-shaping layer, configured as config entries.

example.code:
consul query create -name=orders-nearby \
  -service=orders -nearest=n -failover-dcs=dc2,dc3
example.walkthrough: Create a prepared query with failover; drain local instances and watch queries return dc2.

pitfalls: Failover without capacity planning: dc2 melts when dc1's traffic arrives unannounced.
Prepared queries nobody documents: discovery behavior becomes tribal knowledge.
Nearest routing across expensive links: 'nearest' by latency may mean costliest by billing.
lessons.try_it: Document every prepared query: who queries it, failover order, expected behavior.

lessons.title: Consul ACLs and TLS
concepts: Consul ACLs default-deny when enabled: every agent, service, and token needs explicit grants. Bootstrap with consul acl bootstrap — capture that token like a root password.
Token types: management (god), client (scoped by policies). Service identity policies (service-identity) give a service exactly its own registration + discovery rights.
TLS: verify_incoming/outgoing, auto_encrypt for clients, auto_config for join. Full mTLS between agents is the production bar.
The holy trinity for a secure cluster: gossip encryption + TLS + ACLs. Any two without the third leaves a gap (plaintext gossip, unauthenticated API, spoofable membership).

example.code:
consul acl policy create -name=orders-service \
  -rules='service_identity "orders" { policy = "write" }'
example.walkthrough: Enable ACLs on a dev cluster; issue a service-identity token and register with it.

pitfalls: Bootstrapping ACLs and losing the management token: the cluster is now unadministrable — store it in Vault.
ACLs without TLS: tokens travel in plaintext; sniffing beats the policy engine.
Over-broad agent policies: a compromised client agent token should not read the whole catalog.
lessons.try_it: Audit: does every production agent run all three (gossip encrypt, TLS, ACLs)?

lessons.title: Seal/Unseal and Auto-Unseal
concepts: Seal state: a sealed Vault refuses all operations except unseal and status. Restarts, crashes, and config errors all land here — seal is the safe default, not an error.
Shamir unseal: N key holders, threshold T. Unseal is a ceremony: gather T holders, run vault operator unseal T times. Practice the ceremony before the incident.
Auto-unseal: a cloud KMS or HSM holds the wrapping key; Vault unseals itself on start. Operational bliss — but the KMS is now your root of trust; protect and replicate it.
Seal migration: moving Shamir ↔ auto-unseal requires a migration ceremony with downtime planning. Decide at install time; migration is a project.

example.code:
vault operator unseal   # repeat with T distinct key shares
vault status | grep -E 'Sealed|Shares|Threshold'
example.walkthrough: Practice a full seal/unseal cycle; time how long the ceremony takes your team.

pitfalls: One person holding all key shares: Shamir with a single holder is a password with extra steps.
Auto-unseal without KMS redundancy: the KMS region outage seals you with no ceremony to run.
Never testing unseal: the first unseal should not be during a real incident.
lessons.try_it: Write the unseal ceremony runbook: who holds shares, how to reach them, expected duration.

lessons.title: Audit Devices and Log Analysis
concepts: Audit devices log every request/response (minus sensitive fields, which are HMACed): file, syslog, socket. Enable at least one before production — you cannot investigate what you did not record.
Hash sensitive data: audit devices HMAC values with a salt; keep the salt to correlate, rotate it to break linkability. The log proves WHAT happened without storing secrets.
Audit log volume is large: filter at collection (drop health checks), ship to central logging, alert on patterns (mass revoke, policy writes, root token use).
Blocked audit device = Vault seals (by default): a full disk seals the cluster. Monitor device health and disk space as tier-1 alerts.

example.code:
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
# alert: 'root' token use, policy writes, lease revoke-prefix
example.walkthrough: Enable file audit, perform a secret read, and find your request in the log (note the hashed value).

pitfalls: No audit device in prod: every incident becomes 'we think' instead of 'the log shows'.
Audit disk unmonitored: the seal-on-block behavior turns a full disk into an outage.
Logging everything to one file forever: rotate, ship, and expire — audit logs are also a liability.
lessons.try_it: Build three alerts from audit patterns: root use, mass revoke, policy change.

lessons.title: Storage Backends: Integrated Storage vs External
concepts: Integrated storage (Raft): Vault nodes replicate among themselves — no external dependency, the recommended backend. 3 or 5 nodes, odd quorum.
External (Consul/etcd/ZK): separates storage from Vault, useful when Consul already exists as blessed infrastructure. Adds an operational dependency and a second thing to back up.
Decision inputs: team expertise, existing Consul footprint, cloud KMS availability for auto-unseal. Greenfield → integrated storage, almost always.
Storage backend choice affects backup: Raft snapshots via Vault API; Consul backend via Consul snapshots. Know your restore path for YOUR backend.

example.walkthrough: Deploy one node each way in lab; compare the operational surface (processes, ports, backup commands).

pitfalls: Raft with 2 nodes: no quorum possible — 2-node clusters cannot elect on single failure.
Consul backend with no Consul backup: Vault's data depends on a system nobody backs up.
Switching backends in prod: it is a migration with downtime — choose deliberately at install.
lessons.try_it: Document your backend choice and its backup/restore commands in the runbook.

lessons.title: Upgrades and Version Compatibility
concepts: Upgrade path: standby nodes first, then step down the active and upgrade it. Never upgrade the active first — a bad binary on the leader is a bad day.
Read the upgrade guide for every minor version: storage schema changes and deprecated config keys hide there. Test in staging with production data shape.
Raft protocol compatibility: mixed-version clusters work only within the supported skew (usually one minor). Upgrade briskly; do not linger mixed.
Client compatibility: agents, consul-template, and SDKs tolerate server skew well, but pin and test the auth paths (AppRole, K8s) after each upgrade.

example.code:
# rolling upgrade: standbys, then failover, then old active
vault operator step-down   # on the active, after standbys are upgraded
example.walkthrough: Rehearse a rolling upgrade on a lab cluster; verify leases and tokens survive.

pitfalls: Upgrading all nodes at once: any bug is now cluster-wide with no rollback node.
Skipping the upgrade guide: the deprecated stanza you ignored fails to parse on start.
No staging rehearsal: prod is not the place to discover the new version's breaking change.
lessons.try_it: Write the upgrade runbook: order, verification after each node, rollback criteria.

lessons.title: Monitoring Vault: Metrics and Alerts
concepts: Telemetry: Prometheus endpoint exposes raft, lease, token, and request metrics. The essential four: seal status, Raft leadership stability, lease count growth, request latency p99.
Tier-1 alerts: sealed, no leader, Raft peer loss, audit device blocked, storage disk > 80%. These page. Everything else can wait for morning.
Lease/token growth alerts catch leaks: a steady climb in active leases with flat traffic means clients minting without cleanup.
Health endpoints: /sys/health (sealed, standby, active codes) for load balancers; /sys/seal-status for the unseal ceremony dashboard.

example.code:
# Prometheus scrape of Vault telemetry
vault read sys/metrics format=prometheus | grep vault_raft
example.walkthrough: Stand up the four essential alerts in your monitoring and trigger each in lab.

pitfalls: Alerting on sealed without an unseal runbook: the page fires and nobody knows the ceremony.
No lease-growth alert: the slow leak is discovered at 2 AM when storage fills.
Monitoring the active node only: standby health matters — failover to a sick standby is an outage.
lessons.try_it: Build a Vault dashboard: seal, leader, leases, latency — one screen.

lessons.title: PKI Engine: Root and Intermediate CAs
concepts: Vault's PKI engine is a CA-as-a-service: it generates roots, intermediates, and leaf certificates on demand — no OpenSSL ceremonies, no shared private keys.

Topology that scales: offline root (generated once, stored cold, long TTL) signs an intermediate; the intermediate lives in Vault and signs leaves. Compromise of the intermediate costs a re-issue, not the root.
Generate the root inside Vault or import an existing one: generate/internal keeps the key in Vault; import an existing root when the org already has PKI trust.
Each mount is a CA: mount pki/ per trust domain (internal services, VPN clients, code signing). Separate mounts, separate blast radii.

example.code:
vault secrets enable pki
vault write -field=certificate pki/root/generate/internal \
  common_name=example.com ttl=87600h > root_ca.crt
example.walkthrough: Stand up a root + intermediate chain; verify with openssl verify -CAfile.

pitfalls: One giant root signing leaves directly: every leaf issuance touches the crown jewels.
Root TTL of 100 years 'to avoid rotation': rotation is the security property — plan it.
Forgetting to publish the CA chain: clients cannot build trust without the intermediates.
lessons.try_it: Document your CA hierarchy: which mount signs what, TTLs, and the rotation plan.

lessons.title: Roles, TTLs, and Certificate Issuance
concepts: Roles are issuance policy: allowed_domains, allow_subdomains, key usages, TTL bounds. The role — not the requester — decides what certificates can exist.
TTL layering: role max_ttl <= mount max_ttl <= intermediate TTL. A leaf cannot outlive its signer; design TTLs top-down.
Issuance: vault write pki_int/issue/<role> common_name=... returns cert + private key. Short TTLs (hours/days) + automation beat long TTLs + manual renewal.
List issued certs via pki_int/certs (serial numbers) for inventory; pair with CT-style logging for accountability.

example.code:
vault write pki_int/roles/web allow_subdomains=true \
  allowed_domains=example.com max_ttl=720h
vault write pki_int/issue/web common_name=app.example.com ttl=24h
example.walkthrough: Create a role, issue a cert, and verify the TTL and SANs match the role's bounds.

pitfalls: allow_any_name=true on a shared role: anyone can mint a cert for anything — the CA becomes a forgery service.
TTL longer than the automation cycle: certs expire before renewal runs.
No allowed_domains: the role is a wildcard CA for your whole DNS.
lessons.try_it: Attempt to issue outside allowed_domains; confirm the role rejects it.

lessons.title: CRLs, OCSP, and Revocation
concepts: Revocation: vault write pki_int/revoke serial_number=... adds the serial to the CRL. Clients must actually CHECK the CRL or OCSP — revocation without checking is theater.
CRL distribution: configure crl_distribution_points and ocsp_servers in the mount URLs so clients know where to check. Automate CRL rebuilds (expiry-based).
OCSP is the online check: lighter than downloading CRLs, needs responder availability. For internal services, short TTLs often beat revocation infrastructure — a 24h cert 'revokes itself' tomorrow.
Tidy: vault write pki_int/tidy cleans expired certs from storage. Revoked-but-unexpired certs stay until expiry — tidy does not erase revocation history early.

example.code:
vault write pki_int/revoke serial_number=12:34:56:78
vault read pki_int/crl/pem | openssl crl -text | grep Serial
example.walkthrough: Revoke a cert, fetch the CRL, and confirm the serial appears.

pitfalls: Revoking without verifying clients check: the compromised cert keeps working everywhere.
No tidy schedule: storage grows with every issued cert forever.
CRL URLs pointing at unreachable hosts: clients fail closed (or worse, fail open) on every TLS handshake.
lessons.try_it: Decide your revocation story per use case: CRL, OCSP, or short-TTL expiry.

lessons.title: Automated Rotation with Consul-Template
concepts: consul-template renders certs into files and restarts/reloads services on renewal: the standard automation loop for Vault-issued certificates.
Template pattern: {{ with secret "pki_int/issue/web" "common_name=app.example.com" "ttl=24h" }} write cert/key files {{ end }}. Renewal happens before expiry automatically.
Signal handling: use command or wait blocks to reload (nginx -s reload) rather than restart — zero-downtime rotation.
The template's Vault token needs ONLY the issue path capability — least privilege on the renewal loop too.

example.walkthrough: Run consul-template to issue and auto-renew a cert; watch it rotate without downtime.

pitfalls: Template token with broad policy: the renewal agent becomes a high-value target.
Restart instead of reload: every rotation becomes a brief outage.
TTL longer than deploy cadence with no template: certs expire silently between deploys.
lessons.try_it: Set up rotation for one real service and verify a full renewal cycle.

lessons.title: PKI in a Service Mesh: Consul Connect CA
concepts: Consul Connect can use Vault's PKI as its CA: Connect leaf certificates come from Vault, giving centralized issuance, audit, and rotation for the whole mesh.
Bootstrap: configure Connect CA provider to Vault (address, token, PKI mount, intermediate). Consul then mints leaf certs per service through Vault.
Benefit: one revocation and audit story for service identity; Vault policies control which services get which SPIFFE-like identities.
Rotation: leaf TTLs short (hours); Connect handles rotation transparently. The Vault intermediate rotation is the planned event — rehearse it.

example.walkthrough: Point a lab Connect mesh at Vault PKI; verify service-to-service mTLS still works.

pitfalls: Connect CA token with excess policy: the mesh CA credential should issue leaves, nothing else.
Intermediate expiry unplanned: every mesh cert dies at once — calendar the rotation.
Two CAs (Consul built-in + Vault) in one mesh: split-brain trust — pick one and document it.
lessons.try_it: Document the mesh CA choice and the intermediate rotation rehearsal date.

lessons.title: Transit: Encryption as a Service
concepts: Transit encrypts/decrypts WITHOUT exposing key material: apps send plaintext, get ciphertext. The key never leaves Vault — key management becomes Vault's problem, not every app's.
Use cases: PII fields in databases, encrypting backups before object storage, envelope patterns where Vault holds the KEK and apps hold DEKs.
Ciphertext is portable: vault write transit/decrypt/... works from any client with policy — the data can live anywhere, the key lives in Vault.
Not a substitute for TLS: transit protects data at rest/in fields; TLS protects data in motion. You usually need both.

example.code:
vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/orders
vault write transit/encrypt/orders plaintext=$(echo -n '4111...' | base64)
example.walkthrough: Encrypt a value, store the ciphertext in a file, then decrypt it back.

pitfalls: Apps caching decrypted values forever: transit gives you crypto agility only if you re-encrypt on key rotation.
Using transit where a DB engine fits: encrypting whole rows by hand instead of using proper secret management.
No policy scoping on encrypt vs decrypt: readers who should only write ciphertexts get decrypt too.
lessons.try_it: Separate your encrypt-only and decrypt-capable policies today.

lessons.title: Keys, Key Versions, and Rotation
concepts: Keys are versioned: rotation (transit/keys/<name>/rotate) creates a new version; old ciphertexts still decrypt (Vault tracks which version encrypted what). Rotation is non-breaking by design.
min_decryption_version: raise it to retire old key versions — after re-encrypting data, old versions become undecryptable. This is crypto-shredding.
Automated rotation: schedule rotate calls; alert on key age. Rotation without re-encryption only protects NEW data — plan the rewrap (transit/rewrap) for existing ciphertexts.
Key types: aes256-gcm96 default; ed25519 for signing; rsa variants for asymmetric needs. Pick at creation — type cannot change later.

example.code:
vault write -f transit/keys/orders/rotate
vault write transit/rewrap/orders ciphertext=vault:v1:...
example.walkthrough: Rotate a key, verify old ciphertext still decrypts, then rewrap it to the new version.

pitfalls: Rotating without rewrapping and claiming 'rotation complete': old data still uses the old key.
Raising min_decryption_version before rewrap: you just crypto-shredded live data.
Deleting key versions to 'clean up': destruction is permanent — export backup first.
lessons.try_it: Schedule quarterly rotation with a rewrap runbook for your data set.

lessons.title: Datakey, Random, and Convergent Encryption
concepts: Datakey: Vault generates a data-encryption key, returns plaintext (for immediate use) + ciphertext (stored). Envelope encryption without app-side key generation.
Random: transit/random/<bytes> is a CSPRNG-as-a-service — tokens, nonces, salts without trusting app runtimes' randomness.
Convergent encryption: same plaintext + context = same ciphertext. Enables encrypted database LOOKUPS (equality queries on ciphertext). Requires derived keys.
Convergent caveat: deterministic ciphertext leaks equality patterns — use only where the query requirement justifies it, with per-field contexts.

example.code:
vault write transit/datakey/plaintext/orders
vault write transit/random/32 format=base64
example.walkthrough: Generate a datakey, encrypt a file with it locally, store only the wrapped key.

pitfalls: Convergent encryption on high-entropy-guessable fields: deterministic ciphertext + guessable plaintext = offline brute force.
Using random bytes as session tokens without enough length: 32 bytes minimum for tokens.
Storing the plaintext datakey next to the ciphertext: envelope encryption with the envelope open.
lessons.try_it: Audit where your apps generate randomness; route token generation through transit/random.

lessons.title: Transit for Tokenization Workflows
concepts: Tokenization: replace PII with random tokens, store the mapping encrypted. Transit + a token vault table = PCI-style scope reduction.
Pattern: transit encrypt with convergent=false for the mapping store; the token itself is random (transit/random). Lookup: token → decrypt mapping → PII.
Detokenization is the privileged path: policy it separately. Most services tokenize (encrypt); only the billing service detokenizes.
Batch operations: transit supports batch_input for throughput — tokenizing a million rows one-by-one is a self-inflicted slowdown.

example.code:
# batch tokenize 1000 values in one call
vault write transit/encrypt/orders batch_input='[{"plaintext": "..."}, ...]'
example.walkthrough: Build a tokenize/detokenize pair of scripts with separate policies per direction.

pitfalls: Detokenize capability on the tokenizing service: scope creep turns every service into a PII reader.
No batching on bulk jobs: the API round-trip dominates and the job never finishes.
Tokens that embed the PII (format-preserving without a vault): that is encoding, not tokenization.
lessons.try_it: Map your PII flows: which services tokenize, which detokenize, and why.

lessons.title: HSM-Backed Keys and Key Export
concepts: Managed keys: Vault can use HSM/PKCS11 or cloud KMS keys THROUGH transit without exposing them — the HSM does the crypto, Vault does the API and policy.
Key export: transit/keys/<name> can export (if export_private_key allowed at creation) for migration or HSM backup. Export is disabled by default — enabling it is a deliberate, audited decision.
Compliance story: 'keys never leave the HSM' satisfies auditors; Vault provides the access control and audit trail the HSM lacks.
Seal wrap: with HSM auto-unseal + seal-wrapped storage, even Vault's own storage gets HSM-grade protection. Defense in depth, not decoration.

example.code:
# key creation pinned to HSM-backed managed key
vault write transit/keys/hsm-orders managed_key_name=hsm-key-1
example.walkthrough: Document which keys are HSM-backed and the export policy for each.

pitfalls: Enabling export 'just in case': the capability persists and becomes the exfiltration path.
HSM without redundancy: the HSM is now a single point of failure for all crypto.
Assuming HSM = secure: misconfigured PKCS11 slot PINs and audit gaps still bite.
lessons.try_it: Verify export is disabled on every key where it was not explicitly approved.

lessons.title: Raft Integrated Storage Architecture
concepts: Raft integrated storage makes Vault nodes their own backend: the Raft log replicates every write to a quorum. No Consul, no external DB — fewer moving parts.
Quorum math: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Even numbers do not help (4 nodes still tolerate only 1). Production: 3 for most, 5 for large fleets.
One active, rest standby: only the leader serves writes; standbys forward. Performance standbys (enterprise) serve reads locally — know which you have.
The Raft log is the database: snapshots capture it; autopilot manages dead-server cleanup. Operate the log and you operate Vault.

example.walkthrough: Sketch the write path: client → active → Raft log → quorum ack → response.

pitfalls: 2-node 'HA': quorum impossible on single failure — it is HA theater.
All nodes in one rack/AZ: quorum survives node failure, not rack failure.
Treating standbys as idle: they are your failover — monitor their health equally.
lessons.try_it: Verify your cluster size is odd and spans failure domains.

lessons.title: Cluster Formation and Join
concepts: Bootstrap: first node starts with retry_join pointing at peers; or operator raft join the others to the leader. Use cloud auto-join (discovery) or static IPs — document which.
TLS between nodes is mandatory: cluster_addr uses HTTPS with mutual TLS. Node identity comes from the certs — get the SANs right or joins fail cryptically.
Unseal EVERY node: each node seals independently. A 3-node cluster needs 3 unseal ceremonies (or auto-unseal). The 'cluster is up' check includes all nodes unsealed.
Verify: vault operator raft list-peers shows all voters; vault status on each shows unsealed. Automate this check in your provisioning.

example.code:
vault operator raft join https://vault-1:8201
vault operator raft list-peers
# expect: 3 voters, 1 leader
example.walkthrough: Join two nodes to a leader in lab; break TLS SANs once to see the failure mode.

pitfalls: Joining with HTTP cluster_addr: Raft traffic in plaintext, credentials-adjacent data exposed.
Forgetting to unseal the joined nodes: they sit sealed forever, quorum never forms.
Split-brain bootstraps: two nodes each bootstrapping separately = two clusters. One bootstrap, then joins.
lessons.try_it: Write the join procedure into provisioning so rebuilds are push-button.

lessons.title: Performance Standbys and Replication
concepts: Performance standbys serve reads from local state: lower latency, less leader load. Writes still forward to the active. (Enterprise feature — know the open-source boundary.)
DR replication: a secondary cluster replicates data asynchronously for region failover. PR replication replicates even auth methods and tokens for active-active patterns.
Replication lag is the RPO: monitor merkle-sync status; a lagging secondary is a stale failover target. Alert on it.
Failover is a decision, not just a command: promote the DR secondary only when the primary is truly lost — split-brain writes are worse than downtime.

example.code:
vault write -f sys/replication/dr/secondary/enable \
  primary_api_addr=https://vault-primary:8200
# monitor: vault read sys/replication/dr/status
example.walkthrough: Diagram your replication topology with RPO/RTO numbers per link.

pitfalls: Enabling replication without monitoring lag: failover to a day-old secondary loses a day of secret rotations.
Promoting the secondary 'to test': you now have two primaries writing — test in an isolated lab.
Assuming open-source has perf standbys: it does not — size the leader for full read load.
lessons.try_it: Define the failover decision criteria: who decides, on what signal.

lessons.title: Leader Election and Failure Scenarios
concepts: Election triggers: leader heartbeat timeout (followers notice), graceful step-down, network partition. Raft elects in seconds; clients retry against the new leader.
Partition scenario: 3 nodes, one isolated — the 2-node majority keeps serving; the isolated node steps down. Quorum protects writes; reads on the minority fail.
Client behavior: SDKs and agents must handle 307 redirects and leader changes. Hardcoding the leader's address breaks failover — use the LB or any-node address.
Autopilot: removes dead voters automatically after a threshold. Without it, a permanently dead node blocks future quorum changes — enable and tune it.

example.code:
vault operator step-down          # graceful leadership transfer
vault operator raft list-peers   # watch the new leader emerge
example.walkthrough: Kill -9 the leader in lab; time re-election and confirm clients recover.

pitfalls: Clients pinned to one node's IP: failover works, but nobody can reach the new leader.
No autopilot with dead nodes: the voter set rots until quorum math breaks.
Testing elections never: the first election should not be during the outage.
lessons.try_it: Run quarterly election drills; record re-election times.

lessons.title: Tuning Raft for Production
concepts: Key knobs: heartbeat_timeout, election_timeout, snapshot_threshold, trailing_logs. Defaults suit LAN; WAN/multi-AZ needs looser timeouts.
Snapshot threshold: too low = constant snapshotting (I/O churn); too high = slow restores and long replay. Start at defaults, tune on observed log growth.
Disk is the Raft bottleneck: the log is fsync-heavy. Provision low-latency disks; monitor fsync latency — slow disks cause spurious elections.
Do not colocate noisy neighbors: Raft timing is sensitive. Dedicated disks and CPU headroom for Vault nodes.

example.walkthrough: Load-test a lab cluster; watch election stability under disk pressure.

pitfalls: Aggressive timeouts on WAN: spurious elections cascade into flapping leadership.
Snapshot threshold at 1M with huge writes: restores replay forever.
Ignoring fsync latency metrics: the 'random' elections have a disk-shaped cause.
lessons.try_it: Baseline your Raft metrics for a week; tune once, from data.

lessons.title: Namespaces: Isolation Model
concepts: Namespaces partition Vault into isolated tenants: separate mounts, policies, tokens, and auth methods per namespace. Admins in one namespace cannot see another's.
Hierarchy: root namespace contains child namespaces (ns1/, ns1/team-a/). Policies and identity can be managed top-down or delegated per namespace.
Use cases: multi-team (each team its own namespace), multi-env (prod vs staging), MSP/enterprise tenancy. One cluster, many trust boundaries.
Namespaces are not a security boundary against the root operator: root-namespace admins can always reach down. True hostile-tenant isolation needs separate clusters.

example.code:
vault namespace create team-a
vault secrets enable -namespace=team-a -path=secret kv-v2
example.walkthrough: Create two namespaces; prove a token from one cannot read the other's mounts.

pitfalls: Treating namespaces as hostile-tenant isolation: the root admin is still god — threat-model accordingly.
Flat single namespace for 20 teams: one team's policy mistake is everyone's incident.
Deep nesting without a naming convention: ns1/a/b/c becomes ungovernable.
lessons.try_it: Design your namespace tree on paper before creating the first one.

lessons.title: Mounts, Policies, and Tokens Across Namespaces
concepts: Everything is namespace-scoped: mounts (secret/ in ns1 vs secret/ in ns2 are different engines), policies, tokens, leases. The namespace is part of the identity.
Cross-namespace access: possible via carefully crafted policies in the parent, but rare and audited. Default posture: no cross-namespace traffic.
Token use: tokens are bound to their namespace; the X-Vault-Namespace header (or -namespace flag) selects context. Forgetting the header is the #1 namespace support ticket.
Policy replication across namespaces is manual: template your standard policies (reader, writer, admin) and apply per namespace from git.

example.code:
vault kv put -namespace=team-a secret/app/db password=x
vault kv get -namespace=team-b secret/app/db   # permission denied
example.walkthrough: Apply a templated reader policy to three namespaces from one file.

pitfalls: Same mount path in 10 namespaces, managed by hand: drift is guaranteed — template it.
Scripts without -namespace: they silently hit the wrong (or root) namespace.
Granting cross-namespace access 'temporarily': temporary becomes permanent; audit it quarterly.
lessons.try_it: Add namespace flags to every script and alias in your toolkit.

lessons.title: Namespace-Aware Auth Methods
concepts: Auth methods enable per namespace: team-a can have OIDC while team-b uses LDAP. Each namespace's login path is independent.
Identity groups can span namespaces for central admin teams: a root-level group with policies in each namespace gives break-glass without per-namespace accounts.
AppRole per namespace: machines authenticate within their tenant; role-ids are not portable across namespaces — which is the point.
MFA enforcement per namespace: require step-up auth for the prod namespace's privileged paths while keeping dev frictionless.

example.code:
vault auth enable -namespace=team-a oidc
vault auth enable -namespace=team-b ldap
example.walkthrough: Enable different auth methods in two namespaces; verify isolation of login.

pitfalls: One shared OIDC for all namespaces with no group mapping: tenants can mint into each other's namespaces.
Break-glass accounts per namespace: 10 namespaces = 10 break-glass accounts to rotate — centralize via groups.
MFA only in root: the prod namespace's admin paths are the crown jewels.
lessons.try_it: Map every auth method to its namespace in a single inventory doc.

lessons.title: Multi-Tenant Patterns
concepts: Pattern 1 — team namespaces: each product team gets a namespace, manages its own mounts/policies; platform team holds root and audits.
Pattern 2 — environment namespaces: prod/, staging/, dev/ with progressively looser policies; promotion moves secrets, not credentials.
Pattern 3 — delegated admin: namespace admins manage their subtree (admin policy scoped to the namespace path). Root retains only break-glass and audit.
Chargeback/showback: per-namespace audit logs and lease counts give usage attribution. Tenants see their own metrics; platform sees all.

example.code:
# delegated admin policy (in root, scoped to the namespace)
path "team-a/*" { capabilities = ["create","read","update","delete","list","sudo"] }
example.walkthrough: Implement delegated admin for one namespace; verify the admin cannot escape it.

pitfalls: Delegated admin with sudo on too-broad paths: the tenant admin escapes to root-adjacent paths.
No per-tenant audit review: the platform team owns the blast radius it cannot see.
Environment namespaces sharing auth methods: a dev token reaching prod is one header away.
lessons.try_it: Write the tenancy contract: what tenants control, what the platform controls.

lessons.title: Managed vs Self-Managed Namespaces
concepts: Managed (HCP Vault): namespaces as a service, upgrades and HA handled; trade-off is control and data residency. Self-managed: full control, you own Raft, backups, upgrades.
Decision drivers: compliance (data residency), team size (who runs Raft at 3 AM?), existing cloud commitments. There is no universally right answer.
Hybrid reality: self-managed Vault with HCP-style namespace discipline — the operational patterns transfer even when the platform does not.
Migration path: namespace export/import is not a single command — plan secret migration per mount (KV export/import, PKI re-issuance, auth re-binding).

example.code:
# inventory what a migration must move: mounts, policies, auth, entities
vault secrets list -namespace=team-a -detailed
example.walkthrough: Inventory one namespace completely: everything a migration would need to move.

pitfalls: Assuming namespaces are portable units: they are administrative, not exportable artifacts.
Choosing managed without checking auth-method support: verify YOUR methods exist there.
No exit plan: whatever you choose, document how you would leave.
lessons.try_it: Write the one-page managed-vs-self decision memo for your org.

lessons.title: Connect: Service Mesh on Consul
concepts: Connect adds mTLS identity to every service: each instance gets a certificate with its service identity; proxies enforce who talks to whom. The network becomes zero-trust.
Sidecar pattern: an Envoy proxy runs next to each service; the app talks plaintext to localhost, the sidecar handles mTLS. Apps need zero crypto code.
Intentions are the authorization layer: service A → service B allow/deny. Default-deny flips the posture from 'open inside' to 'closed unless allowed.'
Connect CA: built-in, Vault PKI, or AWS ACM. The CA choice determines your rotation and audit story — decide deliberately (see PKI lessons).

example.code:
consul connect envoy -sidecar-for orders > envoy.log &
consul intention create -deny '*' '*'   # default deny, then allow explicitly
example.walkthrough: Deploy two services with sidecars; verify mTLS with default-deny blocking traffic.

pitfalls: Sidecars without intentions: encrypted but unauthorized — anyone in the mesh reaches anyone.
Apps binding to all interfaces: bypass the sidecar and the mesh policy with it — bind localhost.
No CA rotation plan: the mesh's trust root expires on a schedule you did not calendar.
lessons.try_it: Enforce default-deny intentions in lab; allow only the two flows your demo needs.

lessons.title: Intentions: Service-to-Service Authorization
concepts: Intentions evaluate source service → destination service: allow or deny, with optional L7 permissions (HTTP methods/paths). Identity comes from the mTLS cert — spoof-proof.
Precedence: exact source/destination beats wildcards; deny beats allow on tie. Read the resolution order before writing 50 intentions.
L7 intentions: allow orders → payments only on POST /charge. Method/path scoping turns intentions into API firewalls.
Manage as code: consul intention create in CI, or config entries in git. Click-created intentions drift and surprise.

example.code:
consul intention create -allow orders payments
consul intention create -deny '*' '*'
example.walkthrough: Write L7 intentions for a 3-service chain; test that wrong-method requests die.

pitfalls: Wildcard allows ('* → * allow') to 'get it working': you built an encrypted flat network.
Forgetting deny precedence: your specific allow loses to a broad deny and debugging is miserable.
Intentions only in the UI: the next 'temporary' allow lives forever.
lessons.try_it: Export all intentions to git; review the allow list quarterly.

lessons.title: Sidecar Proxies and Envoy
concepts: The sidecar is Envoy configured by Consul: listeners, clusters, and cert rotation handled via xDS. You configure services; Consul configures Envoy.
Upstreams: declare connect.sidecar_service.proxy.upstreams so the sidecar exposes localhost ports per dependency. The app dials localhost:5000, Envoy routes with mTLS.
Observability: Envoy access logs and stats show per-service traffic, retries, and TLS errors — the mesh's audit trail for east-west traffic.
Resource sizing: sidecars cost CPU/memory per instance. Size for p99, not average — an OOM-killed sidecar takes the service offline.

example.walkthrough: Declare an upstream, dial localhost:5000 from the app, and watch Envoy's access log.

pitfalls: Apps dialing the real service address: bypasses the sidecar, the mTLS, and the intentions.
No proxy resource limits: one hot service's sidecar starves its neighbors.
Ignoring Envoy stats: TLS handshake failures are the first sign of CA trouble.
lessons.try_it: Add upstream declarations and resource limits to every service definition.

lessons.title: Ingress, Terminating, and Mesh Gateways
concepts: Ingress gateways: the mesh's front door — external traffic enters through Envoy with L7 routing to internal services. One audited entry point instead of N exposed services.
Terminating gateways: mesh services call LEGACY (non-Connect) destinations through a gateway that originates plaintext. The migration bridge for brownfield.
Mesh gateways: federate datacenters — service in dc1 calls service in dc2 through gateways with mTLS preserved. WAN federation without opening the world.
Gateway intentions still apply: traffic through gateways is authorized like any mesh traffic. Gateways are choke points, not bypasses.

example.code:
# ingress: external :8080 -> internal 'web' service
consul config write ingress-gateway.hcl
example.walkthrough: Expose one service via ingress gateway; verify direct-to-service access is blocked.

pitfalls: Ingress without intentions: the front door is open to every internal service.
Terminating gateway as permanent architecture: it is a migration tool — mesh the legacy service next.
Mesh gateways without WAN TLS: cross-DC traffic deserves the same crypto as in-DC.
lessons.try_it: Diagram every gateway: what enters, what leaves, which intentions govern it.

lessons.title: Connect-Native vs Sidecar
concepts: Connect-native: the app speaks mTLS itself using Consul's Go SDK — no sidecar, less overhead, but the app owns crypto code and cert handling.
Sidecar: zero app changes, Envoy owns crypto, small per-instance cost. The default choice for polyglot fleets.
Decision: control the codebase and need max performance → native. Mixed languages, fast onboarding, ops-owned crypto → sidecar.
Hybrid is normal: native for the hot Go services, sidecars for everything else. Intentions do not care which pattern issued the cert.

example.code:
# native: app dials with Consul-provided certs via the API
# sidecar: app dials localhost, Envoy does mTLS
example.walkthrough: Run one service native and one sidecar; confirm intentions treat them identically.

pitfalls: Native without cert-rotation handling: the app works until the first leaf expiry.
Sidecars for ultra-low-latency paths without measuring: measure first, then decide.
Mixing patterns without documenting which service uses which: on-call confusion.
lessons.try_it: Decide the pattern per service tier; document it in the service catalog.

lessons.title: Raft Snapshots: Taking and Restoring
concepts: Snapshots capture the Raft log: vault operator raft snapshot save backup.snap. Schedule it (cron + agent token with minimal policy), encrypt the file, ship it off-host.
Restore: stop Vault, restore via raft snapshot restore on a fresh node, unseal. Restoring OVER a live cluster is not supported — restore is a rebuild operation.
Snapshot contents are sensitive: they contain every secret. Encrypt at rest (age/gpg), restrict access, and include snapshots in your secret-handling policy.
Test restores quarterly: an untested backup is a hope. The drill: fresh VM, restore, unseal, read a canary secret. Time it — that is your RTO.

example.code:
vault operator raft snapshot save /backups/vault-$(date +%F).snap
# restore drill: fresh node -> snapshot restore -> unseal -> read canary
example.walkthrough: Take a snapshot, then restore it to a scratch node and read a canary value.

pitfalls: Snapshots on the Vault host's own disk: the fire takes the server and the backup.
Unencrypted snapshots in object storage: you have published your secrets with extra steps.
Never testing restore: the snapshot is corrupt, and you learn during the incident.
lessons.try_it: Automate daily snapshots with off-host encrypted copies; calendar the quarterly drill.

lessons.title: Vault DR Replication (Enterprise)
concepts: DR replication: async copy of the primary to a secondary cluster for region failover. The secondary is dormant until promoted — it does not serve reads.
Enable on primary, generate a secondary token, enable on the secondary with it. Monitor replication status: lag is your RPO, in bytes and time.
Failover: promote the secondary when the primary is declared lost. Clients re-point (DNS/LB) to the secondary's address. Practice the DNS cutover, not just the promote command.
Know the boundary: DR replication is an enterprise feature. Open-source DR = snapshots + rebuild runbook. Both need drills.

example.code:
vault write -f sys/replication/dr/primary/enable
vault read sys/replication/dr/status   # watch last_wal, lag
example.walkthrough: Write the DR decision tree: who declares the primary lost, on what evidence.

pitfalls: Promoting the secondary while the primary still writes: split-brain, two divergent datasets.
No lag monitoring: failover to a stale secondary silently loses recent rotations.
Untested DNS cutover: the promote works, but clients still point at the dead primary.
lessons.try_it: Rehearse the full failover yearly: promote, cut DNS, verify, fail back.

lessons.title: Consul Snapshots and Restore
concepts: Consul snapshots capture the catalog, KV, sessions, and ACLs: consul snapshot save. Consul backs Vault (if external backend) AND the mesh — back it up too.
Restore: consul snapshot restore on a fresh cluster; like Vault, restore is a rebuild, not an in-place merge.
ACL tokens live in the snapshot: encrypt it like a Vault snapshot. A Consul snapshot contains the keys to the kingdom it describes.
Coordinate: if Consul is Vault's storage backend, snapshot Consul and Vault's Raft consistently — document the order (storage first, then Vault).

example.code:
consul snapshot save /backups/consul-$(date +%F).snap
consul snapshot inspect /backups/consul-*.snap
example.walkthrough: Snapshot Consul, inspect the contents, and restore to a scratch agent.

pitfalls: Backing up Vault but not its Consul backend: half the system is unrecoverable.
Snapshot inspect skipped: you do not know what you have until you look.
Same-disk snapshots: the backup dies with the host. Again.
lessons.try_it: Add Consul snapshots to the same schedule and off-host pipeline as Vault.

lessons.title: Disaster Recovery Runbooks
concepts: A runbook is an ordered checklist with commands, expected outputs, and decision points — written for a tired human at 3 AM, not for the architect who wrote it.
Required runbooks: seal incident (unseal ceremony), leader loss (verify election), snapshot restore (rebuild), DR promote (failover), CA compromise (re-issue everything).
Each runbook needs: prerequisites, step commands, verification after each step, rollback criteria, and escalation contacts. Test by having someone ELSE run it.
Version the runbooks with the infrastructure: a runbook for Vault 1.14 against a 1.17 cluster is a trap. Review quarterly.

example.code:
# runbook header template
# Scenario: Raft snapshot restore
# RTO: 45 min | RPO: 24h | Last tested: 2026-07-01
# Prerequisites: snapshot < 24h old, 3 fresh VMs, unseal shares...
example.walkthrough: Pick your weakest runbook; have a colleague execute it in lab while you watch silently.

pitfalls: Runbooks only the author can run: they encode tribal knowledge, not procedure.
No expected outputs: the operator cannot tell success from silent failure.
Stale contacts: the escalation number belongs to someone who left in 2024.
lessons.try_it: Schedule quarterly runbook game-days; rotate who runs them.

lessons.title: Backup Verification and Testing
concepts: Verify three layers: integrity (snapshot restores without error), completeness (canary secrets readable), and freshness (snapshot age < RPO). Alert on all three.
Automated restore tests: CI job restores the latest snapshot to ephemeral nodes weekly and reads canaries. Green badge or it did not happen.
Canary secrets: known values (canary/app = 'chirp') written to every backend; the restore test reads them. A restore that cannot read canaries is a failed restore.
Report RPO/RTO monthly: snapshot age histogram, last drill date and duration. Backups are a metric, not a feeling.

example.code:
# weekly CI: restore latest snapshot, read canary
vault kv get -field=value secret/canary/app  # expect: chirp
example.walkthrough: Add a canary secret and a weekly automated restore check.

pitfalls: Manual 'looks fine' checks: verification must be automated and alerting.
Canary in only one backend: the untested backend is the one that fails.
No RPO reporting: nobody notices the cron broke three months ago.
lessons.try_it: Publish the backup dashboard: age, drill date, canary status.

labs.title: Issue a Certificate from the PKI Engine
labs.objective: Enable the PKI secrets engine, create a role, and issue a short-lived leaf certificate — the core PKI workflow.
steps: Enable the PKI secrets engine: run `vault secrets enable pki`.
Generate an internal root CA: run `vault write -field=certificate pki/root/generate/internal common_name=lab.example ttl=87600h > /tmp/lab-root.crt`.
Create an issuance role: run `vault write pki/roles/lab-servers allowed_domains=lab.example allow_subdomains=true max_ttl=72h`.
Issue a leaf certificate: run `vault write pki/issue/lab-servers common_name=app.lab.example ttl=24h -format=json > /tmp/lab-leaf.json`.
Verify the leaf: run `openssl x509 -in /tmp/lab-leaf.json -noout -subject` after extracting the certificate, or inspect the JSON `data.certificate` field.
Confirm the TTL: check that the certificate's validity period is approximately 24 hours.

labs.title: Practice the Seal/Unseal Ceremony
labs.objective: Seal Vault and unseal it with the threshold of key shares — the ceremony every operator must know.
steps: Check status: run `vault status` and record Sealed=false, threshold, and shares.
Seal it: run `vault operator seal` and confirm `vault status` shows Sealed=true.
Attempt a read while sealed: run `vault kv get secret/canary/app` — expect the sealed error.
Unseal with shares: run `vault operator unseal` with each required share until threshold is met.
Confirm recovery: `vault status` shows Sealed=false; re-run the read successfully.

checks.hint: Unseal with `vault operator unseal` (repeat per share).

labs.title: Recover a Deleted Secret with kv-v2
labs.objective: Use kv-v2 versioning to soft-delete, recover, and permanently destroy a secret.
steps: Write v1: run `vault kv put secret/lab-app/db password=one`.
Write v2: run `vault kv put secret/lab-app/db password=two` and confirm version 2.
Soft-delete: run `vault kv delete secret/lab-app/db` — reads now fail, but data is recoverable.
Undelete: run `vault kv undelete -versions=2 secret/lab-app/db` and read it back.
Destroy version 1 permanently: run `vault kv destroy -versions=1 secret/lab-app/db`.
Confirm: version 2 readable, version 1 gone forever — delete vs destroy, demonstrated.

checks.hint: Write with `vault kv put secret/lab-app/db password=one`.

labs.success_message: Versioning mastered — soft-delete recovers, destroy is forever.

labs.title: Enable and Query the Audit Device
labs.objective: Turn on file auditing and prove that secret values are hashed, not logged.
steps: Enable audit: run `vault audit enable file file_path=/tmp/vault-audit.log`.
Perform a secret read: run `vault kv get secret/lab-app/db`.
Find your request: run `grep "lab-app/db" /tmp/vault-audit.log | head -1`.
Confirm the value is NOT in the log: grep for the plaintext password — expect no match (it is HMACed).
Confirm the request IS logged: the path, client token metadata, and response status appear.
Design one alert from the log: e.g., grep for `secret/data/prod` writes.

checks.hint: Enable with `vault audit enable file file_path=/tmp/vault-audit.log`.

labs.success_message: Auditing live — every request recorded, no secret values exposed.

sections.heading: Policies
items: Policy syntax — in Vault policy evaluation, an explicit deny on a path overrides all allows — it's the carve-out mechanism. The 'default' policy (attached to every token unless explicitly excluded) allows a token to look itself up, renew itself, and use its cubbyhole.

Capabilities — vault policies are path + capabilities (create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny). kv-v2 splits data vs metadata paths: reads need secret/data/..., listing versions needs secret/metadata/...
Policy paths support templating with identity metadata — {{identity.entity.name}}, {{identity.entity.metadata.team}}, etc. 'vault policy read' just shows the HCL source.
Identity-based policies — rule: default + app policies, never app policies alone. Test with a real token carrying the CI role's policies before wiring CI to it.
Common trap — token self-management requires the sudo capability.
Common trap — sudo capability means the policy was written by root.
Common trap — policies use allow/deny booleans, not capabilities.
Common trap — vault policy read shows effective permissions.

sections.heading: Dynamic Secrets
items: Leases — revoking the token also revokes its leases (token → lease hierarchy), which is the bulk path during incidents.

Renewal — vault Agent centralizes the hard parts: auto-auth (AppRole/K8s/JWT), caching (reduces Vault load, survives brief outages), automatic renewal, and template stanza rendering secrets to files (with exec/restart hooks on change).

Revocation — orphan tokens break the link: they survive parent revocation, ideal for long-lived service identities. 'vault lease revoke' executes the engine's revocation logic immediately (e.g., DROP USER in the DB) and invalidates the lease — no waiting for TTL.
Incident response — response wrapping stores the real response in a cubbyhole behind a short-lived, single-use token.
Common trap — token hierarchy only applies to root tokens.
Common trap — static secrets in env vars are simpler.
Common trap — wrapping encrypts the secret permanently.
Common trap — static passwords can't be rotated automatically.
